anchor_text: From ashes ancient Gower is come
summary: Gower presents himself as the ghost of the real medieval English poet John Gower (c. 1330-1408), risen from the dead to tell the play's story. His long poem Confessio Amantis (c. 1390) is the play's primary source. 'From ashes' signals that this is a figure literally summoned from the past to narrate.
detail: Shakespeare stages Gower as a deliberate antiquarian device: the choice of a medieval poet-narrator licenses the play's episodic, decades-spanning story structure and explains the archaic, four-beat verse that follows. Gower's Confessio Amantis, Book 8, retells the ancient Latin romance of Apollonius of Tyre, which is the skeleton of this play. Using the poet himself as Chorus signals that the audience is receiving a venerable, inherited story, not a newly invented plot.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2
Gower's Confessio Amantis (c. 1390), Book 8, is the well-established primary narrative source for Pericles via the Apollonius of Tyre story.
Gower as undead medieval narrator is the play's explicit conceit; 'from ashes' is the standard resurrection-from-the-grave figure; Confessio Amantis Book 8 as primary source is uncontroversial.

anchor_text: ember-eves and holy-ales
summary: 'Ember-eves' are the evenings before the quarterly Ember Days, Church fasting periods; 'holy-ales' are village festivals held at a church ale-house to raise parish funds. Gower is saying this story has been performed at popular religious and community gatherings — it is ancient communal entertainment.
detail: Ember Days (from Old English 'ymbrendaeg') fell four times a year and involved fasting and prayer; the eves before them were occasions for communal gathering. 'Ales' in this period meant a festive occasion organized around drinking, often to benefit a church or guild. Gower's list of performance venues ('festivals,' 'ember-eves,' 'holy-ales') argues for the story's respectable, wide, pre-literary circulation — the very thing that authorizes his right to tell it again on the Jacobean stage.

The identifications of 'ember-eves' as Ember Day vigils and 'holy-ales' as parish fund-raising festivals are well-attested in historical and OED sources, and the rhetorical function — legitimizing the tale by listing venerable performance venues — is a sound reading of the prologue context.

anchor_text: read it for restoratives: The purchase is to make men glorious
summary: 'Restoratives' are medicines or tonics that restore health; 'purchase' here means 'profit' or 'benefit gained.' Gower is claiming that lords and ladies read his poem as a kind of moral medicine, and that the profit of hearing it is to make people virtuous ('glorious').

anchor_text: Et bonum quo antiquius, eo melius
summary: Latin: 'A good thing is better the older it is.' Gower uses a proverb to justify the age of his tale: an old story, like old wine, is all the better for its antiquity. The Latin tag is itself an emblem of Gower's deliberately archaic, scholarly persona.
detail: The saying is a medieval commonplace on the authority of ancient texts. It functions rhetorically as part of Gower's apologia for presenting an old-fashioned tale before an audience of 'latter times / When wit's more ripe' — the irony being that 'ripe' modern wit may actually be less morally nourishing than the ancient tale. The Latin also signals Gower's clerical-literary identity: the real John Gower wrote in Latin, French, and English.

anchor_text: till Lucina reign'd
summary: Lucina was the Roman goddess of childbirth — a title shared by Juno and Diana, meaning 'the bringer of light,' who brings the newborn into daylight. Antiochus says his daughter was born under Lucina's rule, meaning her birth was divinely overseen and perfect.
detail: Ovid dramatizes Lucina's power in the birth of Hercules (Metamorphoses 9.281-323), where Juno sends Lucina to sit cross-legged and delay Alcmena's labor. In Pericles the same goddess is invoked again at Marina's stormy birth at sea (3.1), binding the two births — and the two victims of male tyranny — across the play. Antiochus's invoking Lucina over his daughter's birth is ironic: the 'divinely protected' daughter has been violated by her own father.

anchor_text: The senate-house of planets all did sit, To knit in her their best perfections
summary: In Elizabethan astrology, the seven planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) governed human character and fate; at a person's birth each contributed qualities — beauty, wit, courage, and so on. Antiochus is saying all seven planets aligned favorably at his daughter's conception, endowing her with their combined best gifts.
detail: The image of the planets as a parliament or 'senate-house' deliberating over a birth was a standard Renaissance figure for natal astrology. The conceit compliments the daughter's perfection while also hinting at the play's pervading sense that fortune and the heavens govern human life — the very forces that will punish Antiochus and ultimately restore Pericles. The language of astral influence appears throughout the late romances.

anchor_text: this fair Hesperides, With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch'd; For death-like dragons here affright thee
summary: In Greek myth the Hesperides were nymphs who guarded a garden of golden apples at the world's western edge; the dragon Ladon never slept and killed intruders. To win the apples was the eleventh labor of Hercules. Antiochus compares his daughter to this deadly treasure: beautiful, golden, but guarded by death — the executed suitors' heads around the palace gates are his 'dragons.'
detail: The image is ironic in Antiochus's mouth: he calls himself the guardian protecting a sacred prize, when in fact he is the monster who has desecrated it. The 'golden fruit' that is 'dangerous to be touch'd' is also the daughter he has already touched — a forbidden-fruit paradox that quietly frames the incest before the riddle makes it explicit. Apollodorus (Library 2.5.11) recounts the eleventh labor of Hercules; Hesiod names the Hesperides in the Theogony.

anchor_text: field of stars, Here they stand Martyrs, slain in Cupid's wars
summary: Cupid was the Roman god of love, often shown as a boy archer whose arrows kindled desire; here Antiochus mockingly calls the dead suitors 'martyrs slain in Cupid's wars,' men who died in pursuit of love. Their bodies lie exposed under the open sky — the 'field of stars' is literally the night sky, their only shroud.

anchor_text: death remember'd should be like a mirror, Who tells us life 's but breath, to trust it error
summary: Pericles' meditation on the skulls around him — visible memento mori (Latin: 'remember that you must die') — follows the classical and Christian tradition of meditating on death as a clarifying mirror. The 'mirror' reveals that life is nothing but breath, and to trust in it is a mistake. This is a formal philosophical commonplace, delivered as a philosophical epigram.
detail: The 'death-as-mirror' image belongs to the tradition of ars moriendi (the art of dying well) and memento mori literature common in medieval and early modern Europe. Pericles' reasoning is Stoic in flavor: the sight of the dead suitors should brace, not terrify him, because it teaches the brevity of life. The compressed phrasing 'to trust it error' means 'to trust life is a mistake.'

summary: 'Gripe' means to grasp or clutch desperately (related to 'grip'). 'Erst' is an archaic adverb meaning 'formerly' or 'before.' Pericles says that sick men on their deathbeds stop clutching at earthly pleasures the way they used to do — and he intends to do likewise.

anchor_text: Like a bold champion, I assume the lists
summary: 'The lists' are the enclosed grounds of a tournament or trial by combat, the fenced arena where knights fight. To 'assume the lists' means to step into the arena and accept the combat. Pericles casts himself as a knight entering a formal martial contest — an image that recurs when he actually fights in a tournament in Act 2.

anchor_text: I am no viper, yet I feed On mother's flesh which did me breed
summary: The riddle the Daughter reads is a coded confession of incest: the speaker (Antiochus's daughter) is 'no viper' — a creature proverbially said to eat its mother alive at birth — yet she feeds on the flesh of the one who bore her because she sexually 'feeds' on her own father, who was himself fed by his mother. The riddle identifies the daughter as her father's wife, son, and child simultaneously.
detail: The viper was a Renaissance emblem of unnatural offspring devouring the parent, derived from Pliny's Natural History (10.62), which claims the baby viper chews through its mother's side at birth. The riddle's logic: the speaker is not literally a viper, but she does something equally monstrous — she occupies the role of wife to the man who is both father and lover to her. The closing couplet ('How they may be, and yet in two, / As you will live, resolve it you') makes Pericles the audience and threatens him: solve it or die, but speaking it aloud also means death.

The viper-eating-its-mother emblem derived from Pliny is well documented as a Renaissance commonplace; the riddle's logic is accurately decoded; 'feeds on the flesh of the one who bore her' is the correct reading of the incest conceit in the riddle.

anchor_text: Fair glass of light, I loved you
summary: A 'glass of light' means a mirror or vessel of light — high praise for a beautiful face. Pericles is addressing the Daughter directly, telling her he was attracted to her (the glass) but that the beautiful exterior conceals a corrupt interior. 'Casket' in the next line continues the image: a fine container holding poison.

anchor_text: You are a fair viol, and your sense the strings; Who, finger'd to make man his lawful music
summary: Pericles compares the Daughter to a viol (a Renaissance bowed string instrument) and her faculties to its strings: properly played ('finger'd') in marriage she would draw heaven itself to listen; but played before her time — meaning in the incestuous relationship with her father — the music she makes is hellish. The extended musical metaphor implies that beauty used rightly is divine harmony; used wrongly it is discord.
detail: The viol (viola da gamba) was the genteel instrument of the Elizabethan household, associated with order, concord, and courtly love. 'Finger'd' carries the scholar-level sense of sexual touch — the taboo playing the Daughter has already suffered. The argument formally accuses the incest through a virtuoso extended metaphor (a conceit) rather than blunt statement, consistent with Pericles' need to keep his knowledge ambiguous before Antiochus.

summary: 'Braid' (also 'upbraid') means to reproach, accuse, or expose. Pericles is saying: naming your sin openly would accuse and shame you too directly for me to do it here safely. The word is archaic; modern readers would expect 'upbraid.'

anchor_text: The blind mole casts Copp'd hills towards heaven, to tell the earth is throng'd By man's oppression
summary: Pericles draws an emblem from nature: even a blind mole, burrowing underground, heaps up mounds ('copp'd hills') that signal to the sky that the earth below is over-pressed by oppression. The image means that tyranny, however hidden, pushes signs of itself to the surface. 'Copp'd' means peaked or heaped.
detail: This is a compressed emblematic argument: the mole represents those living under tyranny who cannot see or speak, yet whose very existence casts up evidence of oppression. The implication for Pericles' situation is pointed — he has discovered the king's hidden sin, and that knowledge, like the mole's hill, cannot be fully suppressed. 'Copp'd' (also spelled 'cop'd') means having a peak, a crest.

anchor_text: if Jove stray, who dares say Jove doth ill
summary: Jove (Jupiter) was the king of the Roman gods, famous for his many adulterous affairs. Pericles is telling Antiochus indirectly: even the king of the gods 'strays' into sin, and no mortal dares call him to account — the same immunity kings claim. It is a sardonic argument for why exposing Antiochus's incest would be politically suicidal.

anchor_text: I will gloze with him
summary: 'Gloze' means to speak smoothly, to flatter or gloss over the truth with fair words. Antiochus, in an aside, admits he knows Pericles has solved the riddle — but he will speak pleasantly to him to buy time to have him killed. The word signals deliberate, knowing deceit through honeyed speech.

anchor_text: One sin, I know, another doth provoke; Murder's as near to lust as flame to smoke
summary: Pericles reasons in a tight epigram: one sin breeds the next, and lust and murder are as inseparable as fire and its smoke — where there is lust, murder to conceal it follows naturally. This is the direct reasoning that makes him flee: Antiochus will kill him to protect his secret.
detail: The figure is a paired simile working as deductive reasoning: the smoke-and-flame image is an analogy for causal proximity, not just moral equivalence. The argumentative movement — 'one sin provokes another' — is a commonplace of moral philosophy (the Stoic idea that vices breed and feed on one another), here given brisk dramatic urgency as Pericles decides to run.

anchor_text: sad companion, dull-eyed melancholy
summary: Melancholy was understood in Renaissance medicine as one of the four bodily humors — the cold, dark, earthy humor produced by black bile — whose excess caused depression, fearfulness, and obsessive thought. Calling it a 'sad companion' and 'dull-eyed' personifies the condition as a brooding attendant that never leaves Pericles. The conceit frames his whole opening soliloquy: he is not merely sad but clinically gripped by a melancholic humor that bars both pleasure and sleep.
detail: Elizabethan medical theory, following Galen and transmitted through Timothie Bright's Treatise of Melancholie (1586) and Robert Burton's later Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), held that an excess of black bile chilled and darkened the mind, producing sleeplessness, irrational fear, and a relentless circling of anxious thought. Pericles's complaint that the 'passions of the mind' nourish themselves on 'care' (TLN 230-231) is a clinical description of the self-feeding melancholy cycle Bright describes. The trait links him to other Shakespearean melancholics — Hamlet, Jaques — for whom thought is at once the burden and the mark of a serious mind.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 220

Timothie Bright's Treatise of Melancholie (1586) is a real text that treats fear, darkened cognition, and the self-feeding anxious thought attributed to excess black bile; the page range pp. 102-120 is plausible for the fear and cogitation material.

The humoural reading of melancholy as black-bile excess, the comparison to Hamlet and Jaques, and the link to Bright's self-feeding anxiety cycle are all mainstream and well-supported by the text of the soliloquy.

anchor_text: first conception by mis-dread Have after-nourishment
summary: 'Mis-dread' means misplaced or excessive fear — the 'mis-' prefix marks it as a wrong or misdirected version of dread. Pericles argues that once a fear starts with some cause (however miscalibrated), it feeds itself by worry until it grows larger than any original threat. The word is rare and probably coined or adapted here; modern readers who miss it will lose the logical shape of the speech.
detail: The compound 'mis-dread' appears in no standard dictionary before this text; it seems to mean fear that began in an error of judgment — over-fear, or fear applied to the wrong object. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) notes the 'mis-' prefix functioning as a pejorative intensifier across the canon. The logic is psychologically precise: the initial fear ('what might be done') germinates into sustained care ('cares it be not done'), a self-sustaining anxiety independent of the original stimulus. Pericles is diagnosing his own mental state with quasi-medical precision.

anchor_text: Nor boots it me to say
summary: 'Boots it' means 'avails it,' 'profits it,' or 'does it any good.' The word 'boot' in this sense has nothing to do with footwear; it is an Old English word meaning profit or advantage, still current in Shakespeare's day in phrases like 'to boot' (= in addition, as a bonus). Pericles means: 'It does me no good to say I respect Antiochus.'
detail: The verb 'to boot' (= to avail, benefit) appears throughout the canon: 'What boots it thee to call thyself a sun?' (3 Henry VI). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon lists it as 'to profit, to advantage, to avail.' The word survives in the archaic phrase 'bootless errand' (a useless one) but the verbal form 'boots it' became obsolete. The sense here is purely pragmatic: Pericles reasons that protestations of loyalty are meaningless against a tyrant who acts on suspicion alone.

anchor_text: ostent of war will look so huge, Amazement shall drive courage
summary: 'Ostent' means outward show, display, or demonstration — from Latin ostentare, to show off. Pericles predicts that Antiochus will not even need to fight: the sheer spectacle of a massing army ('the ostent of war') will look so terrifying that Tyre's defenders will lose heart before a blow is struck. The word fell out of common use after the seventeenth century.
detail: Onions glosses 'ostent' as 'outward appearance, show, pomp' (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'ostent'). The tactic Pericles describes — psychological intimidation before battle — was a recognized military stratagem; a large enough show of force could cause a city to surrender without fighting. 'Amazement' here retains its full etymological force: not mild surprise but paralysing astonishment that drives away courage. The argument shapes Pericles's decision to flee rather than fight: resistance is hopeless because Antiochus's power can terrify without engaging.

anchor_text: no more but as the tops of trees, Which fence the roots they grow by
summary: Pericles compares himself to the outermost branches of a tree: the branches fence and shelter the roots below, yet the branches are also the parts most exposed to storm and damage. The extended metaphor captures his understanding of kingship as service — the ruler bears the blows so his people (the roots) can be safe — and explains why his suffering is caused by care for subjects, not self-pity.
detail: The image is an example of sustained metaphor or analogy (a rhetorical figure Renaissance schoolmasters catalogued under analogia or similitudo). Tree-and-root imagery for the political body — the ruler as the exposed part that protects the nourishing base — was a standard figure in Tudor political writing, related to the great-chain-of-being idea of hierarchical interdependence. The logic is paradoxical and poignant: the very care that dignifies Pericles as a good ruler is what makes him waste away ('both my body pine and soul to languish,' TLN 250). Self-sacrifice and vulnerability are the marks of the legitimate prince, as opposed to Antiochus whose rule is purely self-serving.

anchor_text: flattery is the bellows blows up sin; The thing the which is flatter'd, but a spark
summary: Helicanus uses an extended metaphor of fire-making: flattery is the bellows that fans a tiny spark of sin into a full blaze. The First and Second Lords who greet Pericles with empty comfort ('Joy and all comfort in your sacred breast!') are the bellows; the sin already latent in anyone who can be flattered is the spark. Helicanus interrupts them before Pericles can be warmed by the false comfort.
detail: The bellows-as-flattery image is a condensed version of a commonplace in political and homiletic writing about courts: parasitic flatterers inflame their masters' worst impulses. The figure is structurally a metaphor with three explicit terms — bellows (flattery), spark (the latent sin), and the blast that makes both glow. The grammatical form 'the bellows blows' rather than 'the bellows blow' treats the bellows as a singular instrument (standard in early modern usage). Helicanus concludes by naming the flatterer 'Signior Sooth' (TLN 262) — a comic personification that labels him as 'Mr. Yes-man.' His willingness to rebuke the king, kneeling and offering his own neck (TLN 278-279), contrasts sharply with the departing lords and establishes the moral standard the play applies to loyalty throughout.

anchor_text: Signior Sooth here does proclaim a peace
summary: Helicanus coins a mock-Italian title — 'Signior Sooth' — for the flattering courtier. 'Sooth' in Shakespeare's English means truth; but 'to soothe' had also come to mean to humour, flatter, or cajole, so the name puns on both: a 'Signior Sooth' is a man who passes himself off as a truth-teller while actually telling you only what you want to hear. The fake Italian honorific 'Signior' (= Sir, Mr.) gives the flatterer a pompous title that exposes him.

The wordplay turns on that gap: the courtier styled a teller of 'sooth' (truth) is really a soother (flatterer). Helicanus implies that the lords' comfortable agreement is not genuine counsel but a performance of assent.

anchor_text: hark in thine ear -- as black as incest: Which by my knowledge found
summary: Pericles names the secret he discovered at Antioch: Antiochus is having an incestuous sexual relationship with his own daughter, the very woman whose hand he set up as a prize for riddle-solvers. The phrase 'hark in thine ear' signals a stage whisper — Pericles leans in and drops his voice to tell Helicanus what was behind the riddle. 'Black as incest' compresses two registers: moral blackness (the worst of sins) and literal obscurity (the riddle deliberately obscured its own meaning).
detail: Father-daughter incest was among the gravest offenses in Elizabethan law and theology, condemned under both Leviticus 18:6-9 (Geneva 1599, the law against uncovering 'the nakedness' of near kin) and the English ecclesiastical table of prohibited degrees (the 39 Articles). The play's source, Gower's Confessio Amantis (Book VIII), names Antiochus's crime plainly; the riddle in 1.1 encodes it in elaborate mythological metaphor. Pericles's reluctance to spell the thing out even in private — the stage-whisper gesture, the compressed 'black as incest' — dramatizes the unspeakability of the crime while making its nature unmistakable. The sinful father's 'seeming to kiss' (TLN 301) while plotting to strike echoes the play's central contrast between surface show and hidden reality.

The stage-whisper reading, the Gower source, the Leviticus prohibition, and the surface/hidden-reality thematic frame are all accurate and mainstream.

anchor_text: 'Tis time to fear when tyrants seem to kiss
summary: This is a sententia — a pithy, stand-alone maxim or proverb — that Pericles frames as a rule of political life: the moment a tyrant pretends friendliness is exactly the moment to be most afraid, because the gentler the manner the deadlier the underlying intent. In performance such lines were often delivered facing the audience directly, as universal truths detached from the immediate scene.
detail: The rhetorical device of the sententia (Latin for 'opinion, judgment') was one of the most highly valued figures in Renaissance rhetoric, taught under elocutio in school grammars from Erasmus's Adagia onward. A sententia differs from a simile or metaphor in that it is detachable from context and aims to crystallize experience into a general truth — it can be copied into a commonplace-book. The specific content inverts the expected meaning of 'kiss': the kiss of a tyrant is not an affectionate gesture but the Judas-kiss of betrayal. The sentiment is paralleled in Pericles's own observation that Antiochus 'Seem'd not to strike, but smooth' (TLN 300) — the smooth manner and the violent intent are inseparable features of tyrannic power.

sources.name: Erasmus, Adagia
sources.citation: Erasmus, Adagia (1508 and expanded editions): the tradition of collected sententiae or adages as wisdom distilled from experience; the figure was taught in Tudor grammar schools through William Lily's grammar and Erasmus's own school texts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 301

Erasmus's Adagia is a real 1508 work but is a collection of proverbs and adages, not a treatise on the rhetorical figure 'sententia'; the annotation uses it to support claims about the teaching of sententia in Tudor grammar schools, which overstates what Adagia documents — that case would require De Copia, Aphthonius, or Quintilian.

Identifying the line as a sententia is correct, the Judas-kiss resonance is widely noted, and citing the Erasmian commonplace-book tradition for how such lines were received in performance is defensible; the internal parallel to TLN 300 'Seem'd not to strike, but smooth' is accurate.

anchor_text: bed of blackness unlaid ope
summary: 'Unlaid ope' means 'not laid open' or 'not exposed to view' — a double negative meaning kept concealed. Pericles is explaining that Antiochus has shed the blood of many princes specifically to prevent his 'bed of blackness' (his secret incestuous relationship) from being uncovered. 'Lay ope' = to open up, to expose or reveal; 'unlaid ope' = the state of being kept covered up.
detail: The phrase 'lay open' (= to expose, disclose) is common in early modern English; 'unlaid ope' is the preserved negated past participle — 'not yet opened or exposed.' OED records 'lay open' in the sense of 'to disclose, reveal a secret' from the sixteenth century. The sexual resonance of 'bed of blackness' is present but functions primarily as a moral register — the incestuous bed as the seat of the crime rather than an explicit sexual description. Pericles's phrasing keeps the horror gestural: he names the thing through the acts of concealment rather than direct naming, maintaining the same circumspection he showed in the stage-whisper of TLN 298.

anchor_text: till the Destinies do cut his thread of life
summary: The Destinies are the three Fates of Greek and Roman myth (Greek Moirai; Latin Parcae) who spun, measured, and cut the thread of every mortal life. Clotho spun the thread at birth, Lachesis measured its length, and Atropos cut it at death. Helicanus borrows the image to advise Pericles to wait in exile until Antiochus dies of natural causes — or until the Fates decide his time is up — rather than risking a war.
detail: Hesiod names the Moirai in Theogony 217-219 and again 904-906 as daughters of Zeus and Themis; their Latin equivalents, the Parcae (Nona, Decuma, Morta), are described by Catullus and Ovid. The three-part spinning-measuring-cutting structure was a standard schoolroom reference by Shakespeare's day, transmitted through Ovid (Metamorphoses 15.781-798, where the Fates spin the life of Augustus) and through Latin poetry generally. Helicanus's counsel is prudential and pagan in register — wait for Fortune or nature to resolve the crisis — rather than offering Christian hope or active resistance. The image of cutting the thread recurs throughout the late romances as a figure for the precariousness of mortal life against the larger pattern of providential restoration.

sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 217-219 and 904-906 (the Moirai, spinners of destiny); Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.781-798 (the Fates spin the thread of life, Golding's 1567 translation).

The Clotho/Lachesis/Atropos identification, Hesiod and Ovid citations, and the characterisation of Helicanus's counsel as prudential-pagan are all accurate and mainstream.

anchor_text: in our orbs we'll live so round and safe, That time of both this truth shall ne'er convince
summary: 'Orbs' here means spheres of action or appointed stations — the place each person occupies by rank and duty, an image drawn from the Ptolemaic astronomy in which each planet moved in its own orb or sphere. 'Convince' means 'overcome' or 'refute' — to convince someone of falsehood, not to persuade them of truth. The couplet means: as long as each of us stays faithfully within his proper sphere (Helicanus governing Tyre, Pericles travelling), time will never be able to prove either of us false.
detail: The Ptolemaic cosmos placed the planets in nested crystalline spheres (orbs) around the earth; 'orb' for a person's ordained sphere of activity extends this cosmological image into political and moral life — each rank has its proper orb, and to overstep it is disorder. The word appears this way in Troilus and Cressida (Ulysses on 'degree') and throughout the plays as a figure for cosmic and social order. 'Convince' retaining its Latin sense of vincere (to conquer, overcome) rather than the modern sense of persuade is a standard false-friend for modern readers: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'convince': 'to overcome, to vanquish.' The whole closing exchange (TLN 343-347) is a sequence of gnomic rhyming couplets — Pericles's preferred mode for moments of formal resolution — sealing the compact between prince and counsellor.

anchor_text: bound by the indenture of his oath
summary: An 'indenture' was a formal legal contract — so called because the document was cut with a jagged (indented) edge so that two matching halves could prove its authenticity. To be 'bound by the indenture of his oath' means to be held by a sworn contract as if by a legally enforceable bond. Thaliard is saying a man sworn to serve a king is legally and morally obligated to commit whatever crime the king commands.
detail: In Elizabethan law, indentures governed apprenticeships, land leases, and bonds of service — the formality of the cut edge meant forgery was nearly impossible. Thaliard's sardonic observation collapses royal command into contract law: the king's commission to 'be a villain' is as binding as a deed of covenant. The grimness of the joke is that sworn service to a tyrant makes murder a contractual duty, stripping the servant of any moral agency. Onions glosses 'indenture' as a deed between two parties (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'indenture'); the legal sense is fully active here.

anchor_text: unlicensed of your loves
summary: The phrase is compressed and inverted: 'unlicensed of your loves' means 'without having obtained leave from your affection' — that is, without asking the permission of the loyalty you bear him. Helicanus is saying that Pericles departed as if he had not first sought the approval of his people's love for him, which would normally obligate a king to explain his movements to those who serve him faithfully.

'Loves' here means something close to 'loyal affection' or 'devoted subjects' — the political bond of lord and vassal expressed through love rather than mere obligation. Helicanus is diplomatically framing Pericles's secretive departure as an oversight rather than a slight: the king left without officially releasing his lords from their duty to know his whereabouts. The phrasing also subtly flatters the assembled lords by casting their allegiance as a kind of claim on the king's openness. Schmidt glosses 'unlicensed' as 'without permission' (Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'license').

anchor_text: puts himself unto the shipman's toil
summary: A 'shipman' is a sailor, and 'the shipman's toil' is the hardship of life at sea — constant physical labour, violent weather, and the ever-present risk of drowning. Helicanus is telling the lords that Pericles has deliberately submitted himself to the daily dangers of a mariner's life: the next line drives the point home with 'each minute threatens life or death.' For an Elizabethan audience, sea-voyaging was understood as one of the most dangerous occupations imaginable, with mortality rates on long passages that could exceed a third of a crew.

Helicanus frames the voyage as Pericles's penance for having given 'displeasure' to Antiochus — a diplomatic misreading of the real motive (flight from murder), which he cannot disclose. 'Shipman' is archaic for 'sailor' or 'seaman'; Onions (Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'shipman') records it as standard Elizabethan usage.

anchor_text: I shall not be hang'd now, although I would
summary: Thaliard reasons that since his target has already fled to sea, he cannot be executed for failing to kill Pericles on land — and then adds the darkly comic 'although I would,' meaning even if he wanted to be hanged (i.e., even if he tried to fail), he cannot be, because the circumstances have removed his opportunity. He then pivots to a grim consolation: 'it must please the king's seas' that Pericles escaped one death on land only to 'perish at the sea.' The aside is built on sustained dark irony — the assassin finds relief not in justice but in being made redundant by fortune.
detail: The aside develops a characteristic Shakespearean device of the reluctant villain who calculates survival rather than acts from malice. Thaliard's logic chain — 'if I kill him, good; if I can't kill him, sea may do it; either way I'm safe' — is comic in tone but reveals the court of Antioch as a place where moral agency is entirely subordinated to self-preservation. The phrase 'although I would' is also a deliberate absurdity: no one genuinely wishes to be hanged. It functions as a kind of gallows joke (literally), marking Thaliard as a pragmatic rogue rather than a dedicated murderer. The scene ends with him presenting himself as a neutral messenger, having quietly resolved his moral problem by outsourcing it to the ocean.

anchor_text: Who wanteth food, and will not say he wants it
summary: 'Wanteth' is the third-person singular present of 'to want' in its older meaning: 'lacks' or 'is without.' Cleon's question means 'Who lacks food and yet keeps silent about it?' — the rhetorical answer being nobody, so Cleon has no choice but to speak his grief aloud.

anchor_text: Whose men and dames so jetted and adorn'd
summary: 'Jetted' means strutted or swaggered — walked with a proud, ostentatious gait. Cleon is describing a Tarsus that was so prosperous its citizens strolled its streets in elaborate finery, each dressing to outdo the next ('like one another's glass to trim them by'). The word underlines how completely the city's pride has been overthrown by famine.

The image of a whole city 'jetted and adorn'd' recalls Timon of Athens's Athens and the Elizabethan anxiety about sumptuary excess — display without substance — which the famine now punishes.

anchor_text: Like one another's glass to trim them by
summary: 'Glass' here means a looking-glass (mirror), not a drinking vessel. Each citizen used the next as a mirror to adjust and perfect ('trim') their own appearance — meaning the whole city competed in narcissistic display of wealth and dress. 'Trim' carries both the sense of tidying one's appearance and of fine decoration.

'Trim' (OED v. 1, 3) had a wide range from 'to put in order' to 'to dress finely'; the phrase crisply captures collective vanity. The image sets up the moral of the whole speech: a city so given to luxury deserved divine punishment — an argument Cleon himself seems to accept even as he makes it.

anchor_text: Those mothers who, to nousle up their babes
summary: 'Nousle up' (also spelled 'nuzzle' or 'nousle') means to nurse, nourish, or bring up tenderly — to raise from infancy. The word comes from 'nuzzle' in the sense of nestling close for warmth and feeding. Cleon's horrific point is that the same mothers who once pampered their babies are now desperate enough to consider eating them.

The passage echoes the classical and biblical topos of siege-famine so extreme that mothers eat their children (compare Lamentations 4:10 and the siege of Jerusalem); Shakespeare keeps it within Cleon's report rather than staging it, but the effect is deliberately shocking for an audience already alert to Providence and Fortune's wheel.

anchor_text: One sorrow never comes but brings an heir
summary: Cleon personifies Sorrow as a parent who always produces a child ('heir') to succeed it — misfortunes never come alone but breed more misfortunes. The legal metaphor of inheritance (an 'heir' who 'succeeds as inheritor') frames bad luck in the same terms as royal succession, pointedly apt for a governor watching his city collapse and now expecting an invading fleet.

Using them for sorrow underlines Cleon's sense that misery has its own dynasties and laws. The sentiment that misfortunes come in succession rather than singly is proverbial; the classical tradition that evils, once loosed on humankind, follow one upon another goes back to the myth of Pandora in Hesiod's Works and Days.

anchor_text: like the Trojan horse was stuff'd within / With bloody veins, expecting overthrow
summary: The Trojan Horse was the famous Greek stratagem at the end of the Trojan War: a giant wooden horse left outside Troy as an apparent offering, but hollow and filled with armed Greek soldiers. The Trojans brought it inside their walls; the hidden warriors crept out at night and opened the city to destruction. Pericles uses the allusion as a reassurance in reverse — his ships may look like a Trojan horse, packed with soldiers for a conquest, but are in fact loaded with grain.
detail: The story circulated in multiple classical sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2.13-267 is the most detailed and widely read account (Aeneas narrates the horse and the sack of Troy to Dido). Homer alludes to it in Odyssey 8.492-520 (the bard Demodocus sings of it). By Shakespeare's day 'Trojan horse' was proverbial for any deceptive gift or friendly appearance concealing deadly intent. Pericles cleverly acknowledges the fear before dismissing it: the audience would hear 'stuff'd within / With bloody veins' as the expected horror, making the reversal to 'corn to make your needy bread' dramatically satisfying.

sources.name: Virgil
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.13-267 (the wooden horse and the sack of Troy, narrated by Aeneas).

sources.name: Homer

The Trojan Horse allusion is explicit in the text and the reading of Pericles's rhetorical reversal (expected horror turned to benign cargo) accurately captures the dramatic effect; Virgil Aeneid 2 is the most authoritative Renaissance source for the story.

anchor_text: Until our stars that frown lend us a smile
summary: Pericles closes the scene with an image of hostile stars that may one day smile on him. In the Elizabethan worldview the stars and planets governed human fortune: a person born under 'frowning' (malign) planetary influences would suffer until those same stars turned favorable. The image of a Fortune or heaven that can frown and smile drives the entire play, which turns on repeated disasters followed by miraculous restorations.
detail: The image of Fortune or the stars as having a face that 'frowns' or 'smiles' is pervasive in Shakespeare and his sources: Pericles is literally described by Gower as 'fortune's slave' in the source material. The 'until our stars relent' formula is the romance genre's characteristic suspension of hope — the protagonist endures while fate is hostile and waits for the wheel to turn. Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (the turning of Fortune's wheel) is the philosophical framework behind such imagery; it was mediated to Shakespeare through Gower's own Confessio Amantis and through Lydgate, Chaucer, and the Mirror for Magistrates tradition.

The astrological frame of frowning/smiling stars governing fortune is standard Elizabethan idiom and the connection to the play's broader Fortune's-wheel pattern is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: I wis, to incest bring
summary: 'I wis' is a Middle English phrase meaning 'I know' or 'certainly.' It is a hallmark of Gower's deliberately archaic, pseudo-medieval voice. Here it means: 'a better prince who, I know, will prove himself worthy — as opposed to the incestuous king just shown.'
detail: The phrase derives from Old English 'gewis' (certain). Medieval poets used it freely; by Shakespeare's time it was obsolete except in consciously archaic writing. Gower employs it throughout as part of his Chaucerian persona. See also 'I wis' at similar moments in Chaucer. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'wis.'

anchor_text: A better prince and benign lord, That will prove awful
summary: 'Benign' means gracious and good-natured (a standard opposite to tyranny). 'Awful' here means 'inspiring awe and reverence' — not frightening in the modern sense. Gower is praising Pericles as a ruler whose deeds will command genuine respect.
detail: In Shakespeare's English 'awful' regularly carries its root meaning of 'full of awe' — prompting reverence, not fear. Compare 'awful rule' in Richard II 3.3. 'Benign' is a learned Latinate adjective (Latin benignus) used for a prince who is kindly by nature, the opposite of the tyrant Antiochus just shown. The contrast between the two rulers — cruel/incestuous vs. gracious/awful — is the moral frame of the whole Gower chorus. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'awful.'

anchor_text: good in conversation, To whom I give my benison
summary: 'Benison' (also 'benizon') is Middle English for 'blessing' — the opposite of 'malison' (a curse). Gower says he gives his blessing to 'the good in conversation,' meaning those good in conduct and behaviour. 'Conversation' in Elizabethan English meant one's whole manner of life, not just talk.

'Good in conversation' means 'of good conduct, virtuous in daily life' — an older sense of the word preserved in Philippians 3:20 (Geneva 1599: 'our conversation is in heaven'). Gower's blessing is directed at Pericles, who is the 'good' prince implicitly contrasted with Antiochus. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'benison,' 'conversation.'

anchor_text: all is writ he speken can
summary: 'Speken' is an archaic infinitive form of 'speak,' copied from Middle English (compare Chaucer's 'speken'). Gower's line means: everyone at Tarsus thinks that whatever Pericles can say is worth writing down — he is honoured as a man of unquestioned wisdom.

They signal to the audience that this narrator stands outside the present world, speaking from a more distant past. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'speke' and the note on '-en' inflections.

anchor_text: All perishen of man, of pelf, Ne aught escapen but himself
summary: 'Perishen' and 'escapen' are Middle English plural/infinitive forms — 'perished' and 'escaped.' 'Pelf' means money or property, especially wealth gained by dubious means (Old French pelfre, plunder). 'Ne aught' means 'nor anything.' The lines describe the total wreck of Pericles' ship: every person and every possession was lost; only he survived.

'Pelf' is still current in the 16th century, often with a moral edge (see Raleigh's use), but by Shakespeare's time it was already slightly old-fashioned. The stark simplicity of Gower's couplet form — the 'ne aught ... but himself' — is the source romance's way of isolating the hero at the pivot of Fortune's wheel. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'pelf.'

summary: 'Longs' here means 'belongs to' or 'extends' — Gower is saying this action belongs to (or fills out) the larger story he is telling. It is his way of acknowledging that the play's plot is too long to narrate in full, and that the dumb-show and the dialogue must carry the rest.

anchor_text: fetch thee with a wanion
summary: 'With a wanion' means 'with a vengeance' or 'with a curse' — a threatening intensifier. The First Fisherman is warning the Third to stop dawdling and come help, or he will fetch him forcibly. It is a colloquial Elizabethan oath-substitute.
detail: The word derives from Old English 'wanian' (to wane, to diminish) via 'waniand' (the waning moon, associated with misfortune and ill-luck). By Shakespeare's time it functioned as an intensifying mild oath — 'I'll get you, and badly.' OED records it in this sense from the 14th–17th centuries. It is one of the fishermen's first signals that they speak an earthy vernacular utterly different from Gower's formal verse. OED s.v. 'wanion.'

anchor_text: the great ones eat up the little ones: I can compare our rich misers to nothing so fitly as to a whale
summary: The First Fisherman uses an extended analogy — how fish live in the sea mirrors how men live on land — to deliver pointed social satire: the wealthy devour the poor just as big fish swallow small ones. The whale that 'swallowed the whole parish, church, steeple, bells, and all' is a comic fantasy built on the same moral. This device of using natural observation to expose social injustice is a set-piece of popular Elizabethan prose writing.
detail: The fish-eat-fish commonplace has a long ancestry — it is a proverb collected in Erasmus's Adagia and circulated widely in Tudor England, and the image of big fish devouring small as a figure for tyranny goes back to antiquity. The fisherman's expansion of the image — the whale swallowing the whole parish infrastructure — extends it into comic hyperbole, but the moral target (rich misers who consume their tenants and communities) is a live Elizabethan grievance about enclosure and rack-renting. Pericles' aside ('a pretty moral') marks it as a deliberate formal set-piece.

anchor_text: In that vast tennis-court, have made the ball For them to play upon
summary: Pericles describes the ocean as a giant tennis court, and himself as the ball batted back and forth by wind and wave. The conceit turns a gentleman's sport into an image of helplessness: the ball has no agency; it can only be struck. The metaphor was striking and slightly comic — tennis was the game of courtiers and princes, and here the prince has been reduced to the court's own ball.
detail: Royal tennis (jeu de paume, the indoor game) was associated with noble status — Henry V famously received a barrel of tennis balls as a taunt from the French Dauphin. Pericles, formerly a prince, has been battered by the elements into an object rather than a player. The image enacts his fall on Fortune's wheel: he was once a player, now a plaything. The word 'vast' (Latin vastus: empty, enormous, desolate) is a favourite word of sea-description in Shakespeare — see also 'the vast of night' (Hamlet 1.2) and 'the vast of heaven' (The Tempest 1.2).

anchor_text: I'll turn craver too, and so I shall 'scape whipping
summary: Elizabethan vagrancy laws made unlicensed begging a punishable offence; able-bodied 'sturdy beggars' were publicly whipped. If Pericles merely 'craved' (asked politely) rather than 'begged,' the Second Fisherman jokes, he could reclassify his own requests as 'craving' and avoid punishment. The joke is also about the thin line between polite asking and illegal mendicancy.

The joke in the Second Fisherman's pedantic distinction between 'beg' and 'crave' is that legal wording will not save a man from being treated as a vagrant — what matters is whether you have means and a home. The fisherman's willingness to whip anyone who begs (including himself) mocks the harshness of the law. The beadle (TLN 618) was the parish officer responsible for whipping vagrants and minor offenders. OED s.v. 'beadle,' 'crave.'

anchor_text: a fish hangs in the net, like a poor man's right in the law; 'twill hardly come out
summary: The Second Fisherman jokes that the armour stuck in the net resembles a poor man's legal rights — something that is technically there but nearly impossible to extract in practice. The simile is a quick satire on Elizabethan legal access: the poor had rights in law but lacked the money and influence to enforce them. anchor_text: black Ethiope reaching at the sun
summary: Each knight enters carrying a shield painted with a personal emblem and a Latin motto — together called an 'impresa' (Italian for 'device'). anchor_text: Time's the king of men, He's both their parent, and he is their grave
summary: Pericles closes his meditation by personifying Time as the ultimate ruler: Time creates people ('parent') and destroys them ('grave'), and gives or withholds at its own will regardless of what they desire. The language also echoes the de casibus tradition: great men are built up and cast down by Time and Fortune, not by their own merit alone.

summary: 'Countervail' means to equal in value, to compensate for, or to match -- here Simonides worries that the entertainment at his court is not grand enough to be worth what a knight of Pericles' quality deserves. anchor_text: princes not doing so are like to gnats, Which make a sound, but kill'd are wonder'd at
summary: Simonides compares princes who fail to honor their guests to gnats: loud in life, but only remarkable when dead (because then people stare at something so tiny). The simile belittles stingy or negligent rulers -- they make noise but have no real substance, and their only claim to attention is their own insignificance when destroyed. The barb is aimed at persuading Thaisa to honor Pericles.
detail: The gnat was proverbially the smallest and most contemptible of creatures in Elizabethan writing. The surprise at a killed gnat -- 'wonder'd at' (stared at with surprise, not admiration) -- captures the paradox: no one notices a living gnat, but squash one and you pause to look. The comparison quietly inverts the sun-and-stars image of TLN 783-788, where a great king is the brightest object in the sky; a mean prince is an insect. 'Wonder'd at' here means 'stared at in surprise' rather than the modern sense of being admired.

The surface gloss (gnat = contemptible, noisy creature) is sound, but the claim that 'wonder'd at' means merely 'stared at in surprise' rather than any admiration overstates the distinction; more importantly, the reading that the simile is aimed at persuading Thaisa is an interpretive addition not clearly supported by the text, since Simonides is addressing the general principle before giving a direct command, not specifically targeting her attitude.

anchor_text: this standing-bowl of wine to him
summary: A 'standing bowl' was a large, footed drinking vessel -- one with legs or a pedestal so it could stand upright on the table -- used for toasts and ceremonial drinking at banquets. Sending such a bowl across to a guest, filled with wine, was a formal gesture of honor and welcome. Simonides is ordering Thaisa to carry this ceremonial cup to the melancholy stranger knight.
detail: Standing cups and standing bowls were prestige objects in Tudor and Jacobean banquet culture, often made of gold or silver and displayed on sideboards as emblems of the host's wealth. To drink from or receive such a cup was a mark of special distinction among the assembled company. The ritual of sending wine across the table 'pledging' someone -- drinking their health -- bound host and guest in a formal act of sociality. Simonides' command thus has social force beyond a mere request: refusing or failing to deliver it would be a public slight.

anchor_text: He may my proffer take for an offence, Since men take women's gifts for impudence
summary: Thaisa protests that if she, a woman, initiates the gesture of sending a cup to a stranger man, he may read it as forward or sexually presumptuous behavior rather than hospitality. In Elizabethan social convention, women were expected to be passive in courtship; a woman who offered gifts or made the first move was risking her reputation for modesty. 'Impudence' here means shamelessness or immodesty.
detail: The convention Thaisa names was a real constraint on women's agency in courtly culture: unsolicited gifts or approaches from a woman to a man she did not know could be construed as sexual invitation. Thaisa's aside (TLN 821) immediately undermines her decorous protest -- 'Now, by the gods, he could not please me better' -- revealing that she is delighted to be forced into exactly the interaction she publicly disclaims as improper. This double-speak (modest speech, secretly eager feeling) is a convention of stage comedy, but it also captures the real bind of aristocratic women's social performance.

anchor_text: I have heard you nights of Tyre Are excellent in making ladies trip; And that their measures are as exceltent
summary: 'Measures' are formal dance steps -- a 'measure' was a slow, dignified dance in Elizabethan court culture, and to 'trip' means to step lightly or dance nimbly. But both words carry a secondary edge: to 'make ladies trip' can mean to cause them to stumble (an innuendo about seduction), and 'measures' can mean the dimensions of a man's body. Simonides' witty double-meaning -- playing host and matchmaker simultaneously -- signals his deliberate maneuvering of Thaisa toward Pericles.

The verb 'trip' for dancing occurs in Midsummer Night's Dream 2.1 ('we the globe can compass soon, / Swifter than the wandering moon') and elsewhere. The sexual innuendo is latent rather than explicit: 'making ladies trip' could suggest causing women to lose their footing -- a metaphor for seduction -- and 'measures' could glance at a man's physical endowment. The joke, if present at all, is at a scholar's depth; the surface meaning is entirely about dancing.

anchor_text: A fire from heavn came and shrivell'd up
summary: Antiochus and his daughter are destroyed by lightning from the sky, the standard classical and biblical sign of divine punishment for the worst sins. The Greek word for such a death was 'ceraunobolia' — death by thunderbolt — and it was consistently reserved for those who had offended the gods most gravely. The audience of Acts 1 already knows the nature of Antiochus's crime (incest), so Helicanus's report functions as a morality-play verdict: heaven itself has executed the sentence.
detail: Both classical and biblical tradition made death by heavenly fire the signature punishment of gross moral transgression. In Genesis the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed by fire and brimstone (Genesis 19:24, Geneva 1599) for their wickedness; in classical poetry Jove's thunderbolt destroys overreachers like Capaneus (Statius, Thebaid) and the Titans. The detail that their bodies 'stunk' (TLN 877) adds the Roman notion that the unburied or supernaturally blasted corpse was an index of divine wrath — the gods withdrew all dignity. The report is placed strategically: it closes the Antiochus plot-thread efficiently and assures the audience that the play's world operates under moral providence, preparing for the long chain of trials Pericles still faces.

anchor_text: all those eyes adored them ere their fall / Scorn now their hand should give them burial
summary: The people who once worshipped Antiochus and his daughter now refuse to bury them — the ultimate disgrace in both ancient Greek and Roman culture, where proper burial was a sacred duty owed even to enemies. To be left unburied meant the soul could not pass to the underworld and the body was dishonored before all. Sophocles' Antigone and Virgil's Aeneid both show how seriously the ancient world took this obligation.
detail: In the ancient Mediterranean world, burial (or at minimum, the throwing of a handful of earth) was a sacred religious act. Unburied corpses were an offense against the gods of the earth, and the soul of an unburied person was condemned to wander. To refuse burial was therefore not merely social contempt but a theological statement: the gods themselves had voided the person's claim to human dignity. Helicanus's point is that even the crowds who had fawned on Antiochus now feel the loathing so strongly they will not perform the minimal rite. This picks up the de casibus (fall-of-princes) tradition, in which the mighty are cast down utterly — from adoration to rot. The phrase 'ere their fall' implies they still had their admirers at the moment the fire struck, which sharpens the irony: glory and destruction are simultaneous.

The denial-of-burial reading is correct: the text says the onlookers now 'scorn' to give burial, and classical antiquity's horror of the unburied dead (Antigone, Aeneid VI) is the plain background; the de casibus framing (adoration-to-rot) matches the scene's explicit moralism.

anchor_text: his greatness was no guard / To bar heaven's shaft
summary: 'Heaven's shaft' is a metaphor for divine punishment: God's bolt of lightning or arrowed judgment that no earthly rank can deflect. The image draws on classical Jupiter's thunderbolt and the broader biblical idea that the powerful receive harsher judgment, not immunity. Helicanus speaks a compressed moral that is the play's first explicit statement of providential justice.
detail: The phrase 'heaven's shaft' blends two classical images: Jupiter's (Jove's) thunderbolt, the weapon of divine wrath in Homer and Virgil, and Apollo's arrows as instruments of divine punishment (as in the plague-arrows that open the Iliad). The word 'guard' is here a legal-military term — a shield or defense — making 'greatness' a kind of armor that proves useless. The couplet (TLN 882-883) rounds the speech with a sententious, moralized rhyme ('guard'/'reward') typical of the play's choric passages: it states the play's governing providential thesis in the plainest possible terms. Helicanus's role throughout is to articulate the play's moral framework; this is his first such pronouncement.

anchor_text: leave us to our free election
summary: 'Free election' here means the right to choose a new ruler freely — not a democratic vote but the lords' claim that, if Pericles is confirmed dead, the council of nobles may select his successor without being bound by one man's prior authority. 'Election' in Elizabethan political language meant the choosing of a king or officer by those entitled to do so.
detail: In the political vocabulary Shakespeare's audience knew, certain kingdoms were held to be 'elective' — the Holy Roman Empire being the most prominent example, with its Electoral Princes — while England's was understood as hereditary. The lords of Tyre are invoking elective principles: in the absence of a confirmed king or heir, the ruling council reclaims the right to choose. Hamlet uses the same term when the dying prince says 'I do prophesy the election lights on Fortinbras' (5.2) — election there also denoting a dynastic selection by those in power, not a popular vote. Onions glosses 'election' as 'choice, selection; the right of choosing' (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'election').

anchor_text: Whom if you find, and win unto return, / You shall like diamonds sit about his crown
summary: Helicanus offers the lords an image of the reward for loyalty: they will be like diamonds set around the king's crown — jewels that both serve and ornament the monarch. The metaphor works two ways: diamonds are the most precious stones, so the lords are flattered; but gems are set into a crown, meaning they are in their proper subordinate place. The figure neatly resolves the scene's political tension by converting the lords' threatened insubordination into willing ornament.
detail: The crown-as-setting-for-jewels metaphor had heraldic and courtly currency in Elizabethan England; jewels in a crown both derive their significance from the crown and add to its splendor. Helicanus's offer is thus a deft rhetorical move: he elevates the lords (they will be diamonds, not base metal) while reasserting the hierarchical structure they have just threatened to dissolve. The rhymed couplet that closes the speech ('return'/'crown', TLN 919-920) gives the persuasion a sententious finality.

anchor_text: she'll wear Diana's livery; This by the eye of Cynthia
summary: A 'livery' is the uniform worn by a servant or retainer. To wear 'Diana's livery' is to be enrolled as a servant of the goddess of chastity — to live in sworn celibacy. Cynthia is another name for the same goddess in her aspect as the moon: Thaisa swears her vow by the moon itself, making the oath as fixed and bright as the night sky.
detail: Diana (Greek Artemis), goddess of the hunt and of chastity, was the patron of virgins who refused marriage; her 'livery' (the uniform of her household) means a life of chaste service. Cynthia is the lunar title of the same goddess, derived from Mount Cynthus on Delos where she was born. Simonides thus reports that Thaisa has bound herself by double oath: she will wear the chaste uniform of Diana's household for twelve months, and she swore it by Cynthia's eye — the moon, whose constancy made it the classic witness for oaths. Simonides' private aside a few lines later reveals the whole announcement is a stratagem to dismiss the other knights while he manoeuvres Pericles into marriage — so the invocation of chastity is deliberately ironic.

anchor_text: she loves the knight of Tyre! 'Tis the king's subtilty to have my life
summary: Reading Thaisa's letter, Pericles leaps at once to the darkest interpretation: a king showing him a love-letter must be a trap to destroy him. This paranoid aside echoes the real threat that drove Pericles from Tyre — King Antiochus of Antioch, who sent an assassin after him when Pericles solved the incest riddle (Act 1). Having barely escaped one king who wanted him dead, Pericles now suspects every powerful man of the same design. 'Subtilty' means cunning craft or stratagem.
detail: The dramatic irony is sharp: Simonides is in fact plotting, but to marry Pericles to his daughter, not to kill him. Pericles' terror is the psychological residue of Antiochus's murderous pursuit. 'Subtilty' (spelling common in Elizabethan texts for 'subtlety') carries the sense of crafty, hidden malice — the same word used for the serpent's cunning in Eden. The aside reveals how profoundly the Antiochus episode has scarred Pericles: he cannot read a love-gift without suspecting a death-warrant.

Pericles insists he aimed only at honourable conduct toward Thaisa, never at winning her love. The syntax inverts modern word order: 'I never aimed so high as to love her; instead I directed all my services toward honouring her.'

anchor_text: Even in his throat -- unless it be the king -- That calls me traitor, I return the lie
summary: To give the lie 'in his throat' was the most emphatic form of publicly calling someone a liar in Elizabethan usage. A lie 'in the teeth' was direct; a lie 'in the throat' went deeper — it meant the accusation was a deliberate, thoroughgoing falsehood. Pericles is saying he would throw the accusation back as an absolute lie in the face of anyone who makes it — except, cautiously, the king himself. It was a formal challenge that could legally require a duel.
detail: The hierarchy of 'lying': Elizabethan codes of honour distinguished degrees of giving the lie — 'in the teeth' was forceful, but 'in the throat' was the deepest insult, implying the lie was premeditated and cowardly. Touchstone in As You Like It enumerates the 'seven degrees of the Lie' (5.4), the same code Pericles invokes here. The parenthetical '-- unless it be the king --' is Pericles checking himself: he will defy anyone except the one man whose rank places him above challenge. Simonides' aside revealing his private admiration for this answer ('Now, by the gods, I do applaud his courage') shows that the test of nerve has been passed.

anchor_text: either frame Your will to mine, -- and you, sir, hear you, Either be ruled by me, or I will make you -- Man and wife
summary: Simonides builds a comic trap using the rhetorical structure of a threat: 'conform to my will — or I will force you — to be man and wife.' The punishing consequence turns out to be the blessing both parties want. The delayed revelation of 'Man and wife' as the 'punishment' is the scene's comic climax: what sounds like coercion is in fact royal approval. The broken syntax — the repeated 'either... or' and the dramatic dash before the payoff — performs the feigned anger and the glee beneath it.

anchor_text: I'll thus your hopes destroy; And for a further grief, -- God give you joy!
summary: 'God give you joy' was the standard wedding blessing spoken to a newly betrothed or married couple in Elizabethan England — the equivalent of 'congratulations' at a marriage. Simonides delivers it with mock-severity as the final 'punishment,' turning his pretended anger inside out. The phrasing 'I'll thus your hopes destroy... God give you joy' parodies the form of a punishment speech to land the joke.
detail: The phrase appears as a set formula throughout Shakespeare wherever a marriage is completed or announced (e.g. Much Ado About Nothing 2.1, 'God give you joy!'; As You Like It 5.2). Its use here closes the comic reversal: the king has theatrically condemned and threatened the couple only to bless them. The same formula appears in the wedding scene of Pericles Act 3 ('God give thee joy!'). The closing couplet — 'I will see you wed; / And then with what haste you can get you to bed' — completes the scene with an explicit, cheerful nudge toward consummation, the conventional comic end of a marriage plot.

anchor_text: sleep yslaked hath the rout
summary: 'Yslaked' means quenched or extinguished (here, sleep has put out the noise of the revel); the 'y-' prefix is a deliberate archaism — a Middle English past-participle marker Gower uses to mimic Chaucerian verse. 'Rout' means a noisy crowd or uproar.
detail: Gower's chorus opens in a consciously antique register. The 'y-' prefix (Old English 'ge-') survived in Chaucer and in fourteenth-century poetry; by 1607 it was archaic, and Shakespeare deploys it specifically for Gower's voice to signal a medieval storyteller. 'Slaked' carries the literal sense of dousing a fire (cf. 'slake one's thirst') — sleep has quenched the wedding-noise like water on a flame. 'Rout' (from Old French 'route') meant a disorderly crowd; the same word recurs in Antony and Cleopatra for the mob. The pairing of archaism and homely simile (overfed guests snoring, the cat crouching by the mouse-hole) is characteristic of Gower's chorus style throughout the play.

anchor_text: cat, with eyne of burning coal
summary: 'Eyne' is the archaic plural of 'eye,' used regularly in Middle English and revived here by Gower as part of his pseudo-medieval style. Modern English replaced it with 'eyes.'
detail: The plural 'eyne' (from Old English 'eagan') survived in verse through the sixteenth century as a rhyme-word, and Gower — as a character pretending to be the medieval poet John Gower — uses it naturally. Shakespeare himself employs it for archaic effect elsewhere (A Midsummer Night's Dream 1.1: 'steal the impression of her fantasy / With bracelets of thy hair, rings, gauds, conceits, / Knacks, trifles, nosegays, sweetmeats — messengers / Of strong prevailment in unharden'd youth: / With cunning hast thou filch'd my daughter's heart, / Turn'd her obedience — which is due to me — / To stubborn harshness: — and, my gracious duke, / Be it so she will not here before your grace / Consent to marry with Demetrius, / I beg the ancient privilege of Athens'). The homely simile of the watchful cat by the mouse-hole in the firelit house is the kind of domestic image Gower deploys to anchor time and place.

anchor_text: Hymen hath brought the bride to bed
summary: Hymen was the Roman god of marriage and of wedding ceremonies — his name was invoked at every Roman wedding in the ritual cry 'O Hymen, Hymenaeus!' Here Gower names him to say the wedding night of Pericles and Thaisa is over and a child has been conceived.
detail: Hymen (Greek Hymenaios) was invoked at weddings as the personification of the ceremony itself, and his name was an integral part of the ancient marriage song ('Hymeneal'). Catullus and Ovid both hymn him; in Elizabethan stage practice his mention cues the audience that a legitimate, complete marriage has taken place — the 'loss of maidenhead' that follows is the consummation required for the marriage to be legally and sacramentally sealed. Gower's compressed summary — 'Hymen hath brought the bride to bed, / Where, by the loss of maidenhead, / A babe is moulded' — collapses wedding night and conception into three lines, appropriate for a Chorus that must cover months in seconds.

anchor_text: your fine fancies quaintly eche
summary: 'Eche' (also 'eke') means to stretch out or supplement — 'lengthen with your imaginations what the dumb-show only sketches.' 'Quaintly' means cleverly or ingeniously, not in its modern sense of old-fashioned charm.
detail: Gower asks the audience to actively complete the dumb-show with their own imaginative 'fancies': 'And time that is so briefly spent / With your fine fancies quaintly eche: / What's dumb in show I'll plain with speech.' 'Eche' (from Old English 'ecan,' to add to or supplement) is another archaic Gower-word; it survives in modern 'eke out a living.' 'Quaintly' in Elizabethan usage meant cleverly, skilfully, or ingeniously — it retains its earlier sense of 'cunningly fashioned' (from Old French 'cointe,' Latin 'cognitus'). The couplet defines the dumb-show's theatrical contract: the pantomime provides the outline, Gower's verse fills it in, and the audience's imagination does the rest.

anchor_text: By many a dern and painful perch
summary: 'Dern' means secret, hidden, or dire — a Middle English word meaning something conducted out of sight or in darkness. 'Perch' here is a measure of distance (about 5.5 yards), so 'many a dern and painful perch' means the search covered many a hard and hidden mile.
detail: 'Dern' (Old English 'derne,' secret, concealed) is one of Gower's most distinctively archaic words; it appears in Middle English romances and in Chaucer for things done secretly or in lonely, dangerous places. 'Perch' as a linear measure (also called a 'rod' or 'pole': 5.5 yards or 16.5 feet) was still current in rural English, but in verse it evokes painstaking, measured distance — the search for news about Pericles has covered ground step by step. The combination ('secret and painful steps') reinforces the sense that information travels with difficulty across Gower's sprawling Mediterranean world.

anchor_text: Y-ravished the regions round
summary: 'Y-ravished' means 'transported with delight' or 'enraptured' — not sexually violated. The 'y-' prefix is again Gower's Middle English past-participle marker. The news that Pericles is heir to Tyre filled ('ravished') the whole region with joy.

'Y-ravished the regions round' means the news swept through all the surrounding lands and enraptured the people (they respond with clapping and the shout 'Our heir-apparent is a king!'). anchor_text: fortune's mood
summary: Fortune — the goddess Fortuna — was imagined as a fickle power who spun a great wheel, raising and casting down kings at random. Gower says 'fortune's mood / Varies again' as the fair voyage turns to storm: Fortune has abruptly changed her mind. The sea and Fortune are almost identical forces in this play.
detail: The personification of Fortune as a deity with moods — capricious, impossible to trust — goes back to Boethius's Consolatio Philosophiae (6th century), which was standard reading throughout the Middle Ages and known to the historical John Gower. In Pericles, Fortune is the play's governing force: Pericles is driven from port to port, enriched and stripped, apparently rewarded and then struck by loss. 'Half the flood / Hath their keel cut: but fortune's mood / Varies again' uses nautical imagery (the ship has covered half the sea-passage) to dramatize the arbitrariness of the reversal — no warning, no cause, just Fortune's whim. The card for Fortune's wheel is the appropriate scholarly parallel.

anchor_text: I nill relate, action may
summary: 'Nill' is the archaic negative of 'will' — it means 'will not.' Gower says he will not narrate what happens next; the stage action will convey it instead. The word is another marker of his deliberately antique voice.

Shakespeare uses it rarely and always in archaic or heightened contexts. Gower's use here is consistent with his role as a medieval presenter who hands off the story to live drama: 'I nill relate, action may / Conveniently the rest convey.' The couplet is also a rare piece of dramaturgical meta-commentary — the chorus explaining the division of labour between spoken narration and enacted scene.

anchor_text: Thou god of this great vast, rebuke these surges
summary: Pericles calls on Neptune — 'god of this great vast' (the vast sea) — to stop the storm. Neptune (Greek Poseidon) was the Roman god of the sea, storms, and earthquakes, the ruler of every wave Pericles is being thrown by.

Gower's chorus had already personified the sea as 'Neptune's billow' (TLN 1066), establishing the god as the play's presiding sea-power.

anchor_text: Lucina, O Divinest patroness, and midwife gentle
summary: Lucina was the Roman goddess of childbirth — her name means 'she who brings to the light,' and she was invoked by women in labour as the divine midwife. Pericles cries out to her as his wife goes into labour in the storm, begging her to ease Thaisa's 'travails' (both 'travels' across the sea and 'travails' in labour — the word means both in Elizabethan English).
detail: Lucina was an aspect of both Juno (Juno Lucina) and Diana, shared between the two great goddesses of womanhood. Ovid dramatizes her power in Alcmena's agonizing labour: jealous Juno sends Lucina to sit cross-legged, clasped hands blocking the birth, delaying Hercules's entry into the world (Metamorphoses 9.280-315). Gower had already named her in Act 1 ('until Lucina reign'd'). The double sense of 'travails' — sea-crossing and birth-labour — is a typical Shakespearean pun that the scene's staging makes literal: Thaisa is in childbirth on a ship in a tempest. 'Convey thy deity / Aboard our dancing boat' is a brilliantly compressed prayer: bring the goddess of safe delivery onto this lurching deck.

anchor_text: Why do you make us love your goodly gifts, And snatch them straight away
summary: Pericles challenges the gods directly — a rhetorical device called 'apostrophe,' in which a speaker addresses an absent or divine power. He argues that the gods are unjust: they give men beautiful gifts and then immediately take them back, while mortals ('we here below') by contrast do not revoke what they give ('Recall not what we give'), and can therefore claim to deal more honourably with the gods than the gods do with men.
detail: The argument is theologically daring: Pericles inverts the standard relationship of mortals to gods, claiming moral superiority in the transaction of gifts. 'Recall not what we give' — we humans do not repossess our presents — 'and therein may / Use honour with you' (in this respect we can claim to deal honourably with you). The compressed logic is: if giving and not taking back is honour, mortals are more honourable than the gods who take their gifts. This paradox — mortals outdoing the gods in fidelity — is central to Pericles's character and to the play's romance pattern, in which the gods do in fact ultimately restore what they took.

anchor_text: For a more blustrous birth had never babe
summary: Pericles's address to his newborn daughter is a blessing spoken in the form of an elegy — the four lines make a series of antitheses between the violence of her birth ('blustrous,' 'chiding,' 'the rudliest welcome') and the gentleness he wishes for her life ('mild,' 'quiet and gentle'). The rhetorical pattern is called 'antithesis,' and it names the child's defining contradiction: born of storm, she is wished into calm.
detail: 'Blustrous' (blusterous, stormy) is a Shakespeare coinage used only here. 'Chiding' means scolding or stormy (the sky 'chides' with thunder); 'conditions' means qualities or temperament. 'Rudliest' (roughest, most violent) is the superlative of 'rudle' — OED marks it as rare and probably a Shakespeare invention. 'Portage' (TLN 1121) means what can be carried or borne: 'thy loss is more than can thy portage quit' means the grief of losing Thaisa is more than any good fortune the baby can compensate for. The blessing-over-the-newborn is a traditional set-piece in romance narrative (compare Perdita's exposure in The Winter's Tale); here it is charged with Pericles's barely controlled grief.

The identification of antithesis as the governing figure is sound, and most of the glosses are correct, but the claim that 'portage' means 'capacity to compensate' at TLN 1121 is contested — the more widely accepted reading is 'what you carry / what you bring' (i.e. the baby cannot by her mere existence compensate for Thaisa's loss), which is a shade different from 'capacity to compensate'; the annotation's gloss is not wrong but represents one editorial reading among several

anchor_text: your queen must overboard: the sea works high
summary: The sailors insist that a corpse aboard ship during a storm brings bad luck and that the sea will not lie still until the ship is 'cleared of the dead.' This was a widespread superstition among early modern European mariners: a body on deck was thought to anger the sea-god and prolong the storm.
detail: The First Sailor says: 'with us at sea it has been still observed; and we are strong in custom.' The 'custom' of throwing a corpse overboard to calm a storm is attested in multiple early modern sources on seafaring belief. The belief may derive from the taboo against bringing the dead into sacred space — the ship as a kind of enclosed community — or from older sacrificial logic (the sea requires an offering). Pericles calls it 'superstition' (a precise Reformation-era term meaning irrational or un-Christian belief), but then acquiesces: 'As you think meet.' His compliance is practically driven — he cannot keep the ship in the storm to observe funeral rites — but his farewell speech (TLN 1142-1155) shows how much it costs him.

sources.name: Hakluyt, Principal Navigations
sources.citation: Richard Hakluyt, The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques and Discoveries of the English Nation (1598-1600): multiple accounts of sea-burials as both emergency custom and superstitious obligation among mariners.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1134

Hakluyt's Principal Navigations (1598-1600) is a real work, but no specific passage in it documenting the superstition that a corpse must be thrown overboard to calm a storm could be confirmed; the citation is plausible but unverified for this precise claim.

The superstition that a corpse at sea prolongs a storm is accurately described as a widespread early modern maritime belief, and Pericles's own word 'superstition' in the text confirms the annotation's framing.

anchor_text: the unfriendly elements Forgot thee utterly
summary: Pericles laments that Thaisa cannot have a proper burial: no church, no candles, no grave, no ceremony — just a chest thrown into the sea. Elizabethans believed a Christian burial in consecrated ground was essential for the soul's dignity, and to be 'cast into the ooze' with no rite was a genuine deprivation, not merely a practical inconvenience.
detail: 'Hallow'd to thy grave' means consecrated or given a sacred burial rite. 'E'er-remaining lamps' alludes to the tradition of keeping a perpetual light burning over a tomb — candles or oil-lamps left as monuments — which Thaisa will not have; instead, 'the belching whale / And humming water must o'erwhelm thy corpse, / Lying with simple shells.' The image of shell-strewn bones on the sea-bed is a bitter anti-elegy: it contrasts the elaborate funeral monuments of the aristocracy (carved stone, inscriptions, undying flame) with the most anonymous of deaths. The speech prepares the audience for Thaisa's miraculous recovery in Ephesus: the sea that should have been her tomb becomes instead the vessel of her restoration.
