fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1143

OED s.v. 'hallow' is fine, but Camden's Remains Concerning Britain (1605) — primarily a work on language, names, proverbs, and epitaphs — is not a standard source for documentation of perpetual funerary lamp customs, and no evidence was found that it contains the specific content cited.

The reading of the funeral-deprivation lament (no candles, no grave, no ceremony) as reflecting the Elizabethan belief in the dignity of proper Christian burial is sound, and the anti-elegy interpretation of 'shell-strewn bones' as preparation for the miraculous recovery is a standard critical reading.

anchor_text: Bid Nestor bring me spices, ink and paper
summary: Pericles orders aromatic spices (to slow decomposition and honour the dead), writing materials, and a 'satin coffer' — a padded chest. These are the requirements for an emergency sea-burial that tries to preserve some dignity: spices embalm, the written note identifies the body, and the chest keeps it sealed. The combination also sets up the miracle of the next scene, where the caulked and sealed chest washes ashore.
detail: Ancient and early modern burial practice used spices both practically (to slow decay and mask the smell) and symbolically (as precious offerings: myrrh and aloes for embalming are mentioned in John 19:39-40 for Christ's burial, so the gesture carries a sacred resonance). The ink and paper allow Pericles to write a note identifying Thaisa for whoever finds the chest — a practical detail that becomes the plot mechanism: in 3.2, the note Cerimon finds identifies her. The Second Sailor has already reported 'a chest beneath the hatches, caulked and bitumed ready' — caulked (sealed with oakum and pitch) to keep water out, the nautical term 'bitumed' (pitched) underscoring that the sailors are well-prepared for this contingency.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1151

The practical reading (spices to embalm, ink/paper to identify the body, caulked chest as the plot mechanism for 3.2) is accurate; the John 19:39-40 parallel for spices as sacred honour for the dead is defensible without being over-read.

anchor_text: Give this to the 'pothecary
summary: 'Pothecary is an aphetic (clipped) form of 'apothecary' — the early-modern term for a pharmacist or druggist who prepared and dispensed medicines. Cerimon sends a prescription to be compounded, establishing from the start that his household runs on professional medical practice, not folk magic.
detail: The apothecary was a licensed medical tradesman ranked below the physician: he prepared compound remedies from animal, vegetable, and mineral ingredients (the very categories Cerimon itemizes at TLN 1207-1208). In Romeo and Juliet the apothecary who sells Romeo the poison operates under the same guild. The clipped form ''pothecary' (dropping the initial syllable) was standard colloquial usage recorded in Onions and Schmidt.

anchor_text: Virtue and cunning were endowments greater
summary: Here 'cunning' means 'skill, learning, practical knowledge,' not deception. Cerimon argues that inner qualities — moral virtue and acquired expertise — are worth more than inherited rank or wealth ('nobleness and riches'), because heirs can fritter away money but no one can take away what a person knows.
detail: In early modern English 'cunning' regularly meant learned skill or craft (from Old English cunnan, 'to know'). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon lists 'knowledge, skill, art' as the primary sense. The word's connotation of clever trickery was already developing, but in formal moral statements like this one the neutral sense of expertise dominates. Cerimon's speech is the play's first explicit statement of its theme: that healing art and charity — not power or money — constitute the good life and confer lasting renown.

anchor_text: studied physic, through which secret art
summary: 'Physic' means medicine — the healing art as a whole. Cerimon says he has spent his life studying it, reading 'authorities' (medical texts), and so gained mastery over 'the blest infusions / That dwell in vegetives, in metals, stones': healing properties resident in plants, minerals, and gemstones. This describes the three kingdoms of nature recognized by Renaissance natural philosophy as the sources of all medicines.
detail: The phrase 'vegetives, metals, stones' maps directly onto the three kingdoms of the natural world that Paracelsian and Galenic physicians both catalogued as the material basis of pharmacy. 'Vegetives' (plants) supplied herbs, barks, and resins; metals (mercury, antimony, gold) were the basis of Paracelsian chemical medicine; stones or minerals were ground for preparations. Calling these 'blest infusions' frames Cerimon's art as a gift from God rather than mere technique — an echo of the providential medicine that will revive Thaisa. The 'turning o'er authorities' means reading the classical and contemporary medical canon: Galen, Dioscorides, Pliny's Natural History, and their Renaissance successors.

anchor_text: Or tie my treasure up in silken bags, To please the fool and death
summary: 'The fool and death' is a proverbial pairing from the medieval allegory the Dance of Death (Latin Danse Macabre), in which Death leads all ranks — kings, fools, beggars — in an equal procession to the grave. To hoard gold only 'to please the fool and death' means that wealth ultimately serves only two masters: the man foolish enough to inherit it and Death, who takes it all in the end.
detail: The Dance of Death, widely depicted in late-medieval church murals and in woodcut books (notably Holbein's Totentanz series, first published 1538), showed Death leading representatives of every social rank. 'The fool' here likely glances at the 'careless heirs' of TLN 1200 who squander wealth. The pairing sardonic ally punctures the miser's fantasy: gold stored in silk bags is kept, not used, and ends up amusing either a wastrel or the worm. Cerimon's counter-example — spending his 'purse' on his neighbours' health — is the play's normative alternative.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

Invoking the Danse Macabre as the specific referent is a plausible but not necessary reading — 'the fool and death' may simply be a proverbial collocation meaning 'the foolish heir and the grave' without requiring the medieval allegorical tradition; the annotation overstates the Danse Macabre connection (which is one interpretive possibility, not the plain sense) and the confidence of 'medium' is appropriate, but the Holbein gloss goes further than the text warrants.

anchor_text: How close 'tis caulk'd and bitumed
summary: To 'caulk' a joint means to pack it with fibrous material (oakum — tarred rope-fibre) and then seal it with pitch or bitumen ('bitumed') so that no water can enter. Cerimon is noting that the chest has been made watertight to exactly the same standard as a ship's hull — which explains how Thaisa's body survived a sea-storm intact.
detail: Bitumen (mineral tar or pitch) was the standard sealant for ship planking. The detail is carefully realistic: Pericles had the chest prepared quickly in 3.1, and the sailors insisted on casting it overboard because of a superstition about keeping a corpse at sea — but someone (or the text implies Pericles himself) ensured it was sealed against water. The close caulking also helps explain why the body is fresh enough to revive.

The lexical glosses are accurate, and the inference that close caulking helps explain the body's freshness is a reasonable dramatic reading of the staging logic, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Shrouded in cloth of state; balm'd and entreasured With full bags of spices
summary: 'Cloth of state' is the richly embroidered fabric reserved for canopies over thrones and for dressing the bodies of royalty. 'Balm'd' means embalmed with aromatic oils and resins; spices (cinnamon, myrrh, cloves) were packed around a body both to preserve it and to signal high rank. Together these details identify Thaisa to Cerimon as a person of the highest status even before he reads the scroll.
detail: Embalming with spiced oils and wrapping in fine cloth was the recognized burial rite for royalty and great nobles in the ancient and medieval Mediterranean world — and in Elizabethan England for state funerals. The spices also recall the biblical account of Christ's burial, in which Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes. The dramatic irony is that this burial preparation, meant to preserve a corpse, accidentally preserves a living woman: the very care Pericles took in 3.1 becomes the material cause of Thaisa's survival.

The identification of 'cloth of state' as royal-funeral fabric and 'balm'd' as embalming is correct; the observation that burial preparation becomes the means of survival is a sound dramatic irony reading, not an interpolation.

anchor_text: Apollo, perfect me in the characters
summary: Apollo was the Greek and Roman god of the sun, music, healing, and — above all — prophecy and divination: the god who speaks truth and illuminates what is hidden. Cerimon asks him to help read the writing ('characters' = letters, written signs) on the scroll. Invoking Apollo to help decipher a message fits his role as the god who reveals and interprets.
detail: Apollo's oracular function was centred on his great shrine at Delphi, where the Pythia delivered divinely inspired responses. As a god of light and truth he was also invoked as a patron of literacy and accurate reading. The word 'characters' in early modern English means written letters or signs (from Greek kharaktir, 'engraved mark'), not personality traits. Cerimon's appeal simultaneously positions him as a literate, learned physician in the tradition of Apollo's healing aspect (see Aesculapius, Apollo's son) and marks this moment as one of miraculous revelation — what the scroll says will, in fact, prove both true and providential.

anchor_text: I heard of an Egyptian That had nine hours lien dead
summary: Cerimon cites a medical precedent: an Egyptian person who appeared dead for nine hours was revived by 'good appliance' — proper treatment. He uses this case to justify attempting to resuscitate Thaisa, arguing that death can 'usurp on nature' for a time before the vital fire is completely extinguished. 'Lien dead' means 'lain dead' (the archaic past participle of 'lie').
detail: Shakespeare draws on the ancient and Renaissance medical tradition of apparent death — states of deep catalepsy, trance, or hypothermia that could be mistaken for actual death. Pliny the Elder records several cases of persons who revived after being laid out for burial (Natural History 7.52). The anecdote serves a precise dramatic function: it licenses the audience to accept the revival of Thaisa not as a miracle but as medicine, while the atmosphere of spices, fire, music, and Aesculapius's name at the close keeps the scene hovering between the rational and the sacred.

anchor_text: The rough and woeful music that we have, Cause it to sound
summary: Cerimon orders music played alongside the fire and cloths as part of the revival. Renaissance medical theory held that music could restore vital spirits by sympathetically resonating with the body's own rhythms — 'rough and woeful' suggests the viol music is loud and plaintive rather than gentle, intended to rouse rather than soothe. The viol (a bowed string instrument) was the standard indoor consort instrument of the period.
detail: The idea that music could cure illness descended from Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy (the harmony of the soul corresponding to musical harmony) through Galenic medicine and into early modern medical practice. Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) devotes a section to music as a medical remedy; the tradition was well established before that. The viol ('viol once more') suggests a bass viol or consort of viols — the leading chamber instruments of Elizabethan England before the violin family displaced them. In this scene music works alongside heat (fire and warm cloths) and fresh air ('give her air') as three-part resuscitation: a recognizably systematic, if archaic, procedure.

anchor_text: she gins to blow Into life's flower again
summary: 'Gins' is an archaic contraction of 'begins' (from Old English ginnan, 'to begin'). So Cerimon is saying: 'she begins to breathe into life's flower again' — the first signs of breath returning. The image of 'life's flower' compares the renewed breath to a flower opening, a small but vivid emblem of revival.
detail: The form 'gin / gins / gan' for begin was common in medieval and early modern verse — it survives longest in deliberately archaic contexts. Gower the Chorus uses it freely elsewhere in Pericles (e.g. 'gins' in 4.chorus). Here in Cerimon's prose the word has slipped from formal verse into excited speech, which underlines how quickly Cerimon is narrating what he sees in real time. The flower-metaphor continues the scene's imagery of nature reviving: earlier the gentlemen describe Cerimon as someone who makes 'nature conversant with pain'; now 'life's flower' opening is nature reasserting itself against death.

anchor_text: Her eyelids, cases to those heavenly jewels Which Pericles hath lost
summary: Cerimon describes Thaisa's eyes as 'heavenly jewels' locked inside the case of her eyelids — a conceit (an extended, elaborate comparison) that also identifies them as Pericles' lost treasure: eyes that belong, through marriage, to her husband. 'The diamonds of a most praised water' continues the gem metaphor: diamonds of the finest 'water' (clarity and brilliance) are the highest-quality stones, here meaning irises of extraordinary beauty.
detail: The 'water' of a precious stone was the technical jeweller's term for its degree of transparency and lustre: a diamond of the 'first water' or 'most praised water' was perfectly clear and brilliant. The metaphor layers two registers: Thaisa's eyes are priceless gems that have been locked away (eyes shut = jewel-case closed) and that will, when they open, 'make the world twice rich' — enriched both by her beauty and by the reunion they will eventually enable. The conceit is characteristic of the late romances, where extravagant, jewel-laden imagery signals a moment of miraculous restoration.

anchor_text: O dear Diana
summary: Diana — goddess of the moon, chastity, and the hunt — is the presiding deity of Pericles. Thaisa's first words on reviving are an invocation of Diana, which is the play's first signal that she will become Diana's votaress (priestess) at Ephesus, where Diana had her greatest temple. The revival itself takes place in Ephesus, Diana's sacred city.
detail: Ephesus was famous throughout the ancient world for the Temple of Artemis (Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. That Thaisa wakes calling on Diana is not accidental: the rest of the play will see her enter Diana's service as a vestal, and the final reunion of the family occurs at Diana's temple. Thaisa's cry also echoes the play's association of chastity and miraculous restoration — Diana is the guarantor of the purity that survived the brothel (Marina) and the sea-death (Thaisa). In Ovid Diana was identified with Luna (the moon) and Hecate (the underworld), so she governs both the night-darkness of apparent death and the silvery light of revival.

sources.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 918 (Artemis/Diana); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.155-252 (Diana the chaste huntress). For Ephesus as the seat of Diana's great temple: Pliny, Natural History 36.21.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1288

That Thaisa's first words invoke Diana is pointedly significant given that she becomes Diana's priestess at Ephesus and the reunion occurs at Diana's temple — the annotation's interpretation is consistent with the play's explicit later action, not a projection.

anchor_text: AEsculapius guide us
summary: Aesculapius (Greek Asklepios) was the god of medicine and healing in classical antiquity, son of Apollo. Cerimon's closing prayer asks Aesculapius to guide him as he carries Thaisa to recovery. The invocation is the scene's final touch: Cerimon frames his medical skill as divinely aided, not self-sufficient.
detail: In classical myth Aesculapius was so skilled a healer that he raised the dead — whereupon Hades complained and Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt to restore the natural order. His symbol, the staff with a serpent coiled around it (the caduceus in popular usage, but strictly the Rod of Asclepius), remains the emblem of medicine today. Shakespeare invokes him in Cymbeline as well (5.5, 'Thou art not so unkind / As man's ingratitude; Aesculapius' in some editions; 'Aesculapius' in the late romances generally). Cerimon invoking both Apollo (TLN 1245) and Aesculapius in the same scene is pointed: father and son, the twin classical patrons of prophecy and healing, bracket the scroll-reading and the revival.

Ovid Met. 15.622-744 confirmed (Aesculapius brings his serpent-form to Rome; the raising-the-dead myth is present in this book); Virgil Aen. 7.769-771 confirmed (Hippolytus raised by Aesculapius, Jupiter strikes him with a thunderbolt for raising the dead).

The identification of Aesculapius as the god of medicine, son of Apollo, and the observation that Apollo (TLN 1245) and Aesculapius bracket the scene are correct and interpretively sound; the parenthetical Cymbeline parallel is accurate but the claim about 'caduceus' vs 'Rod of Asclepius' is a pedantic aside that does not affect the verdict.

anchor_text: litigious peace
summary: 'Litigious peace' means a peace that is disputed or insecure — contested, as if it could be argued away in court at any moment. Tyre is at peace, but Pericles says that peace is fragile and contested, so he must return to govern.
detail: The adjective 'litigious' derives from Latin litigiosus (given to lawsuits, contentious). In Shakespeare's usage it extends beyond legal disputes to mean 'quarrelsome' or 'unsettled' more generally (OED s.v. 'litigious' 2). The compressed phrase catches the political tension of Pericles' absence from Tyre: not an active war, but a peace uncertain enough to require the prince's presence.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'litigious' adj. 2: 'given to litigation; contentious, disputatious; also, of things: disputed, contested' (first attested senses from 16th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1299
OED s.v. 'litigious' adj. 2 is a genuine entry covering the extended sense 'disputed, contested' from the 16th century, and accurately supports the claim.
OED sense 2 ('disputed, contested') is legitimate and the reading that Tyre's peace is fragile and contested is a mainstream, defensible gloss of the compressed phrase.

anchor_text: shafts of fortune, though they hurt you mortally
summary: Cleon imagines Fortune as an archer shooting arrows ('shafts') at random. The image comes from the classical figure of Fortune — blind, capricious — who wounds some people dead-on and only 'glances' (grazes) others. Pericles has been mortally struck (Thaisa dead, Marina an orphan infant); Cleon and Dionyza have merely been grazed.
detail: Fortune as an archer was a standard variant of the Fortune's-wheel image in late-antique and medieval tradition; Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (Book II) treats her as an active force raining blows on mortals. 'Glance' here means 'strike at a slant, graze' — the shaft that might have killed Cleon has only nicked him, whereas Pericles has taken the full shot. 'Wanderingly' (erratically, at random) reinforces Fortune's blindness: she does not aim deliberately. The speech is Cleon's clumsy attempt to express sympathy — acknowledging that Pericles' loss is far greater than anything Tarsus has suffered.

sources.name: Boethius
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (Fortune and her blows against mortals — the standard late-antique account of Fortune's agency).

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'glance': 'to strike obliquely, to touch lightly in passing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1302

Boethius Consolatio II, prose 1-2 does present Fortune as an active force dealing blows to mortals, and Schmidt s.v. 'glance' for oblique/grazing strike is standard lexicography; the archer-variant claim is a reasonable extension of the Boethian Fortune-as-aggressor.

Fortune-as-archer is a well-attested classical and medieval image; 'glance' meaning 'strike obliquely' is confirmed by Schmidt and the OED; the reading of comparative suffering (Pericles mortally struck vs. Cleon merely grazed) is sound and follows directly from the text.

anchor_text: If neglection Should therein make me vile
summary: 'Neglection' is an archaic noun meaning 'neglect' or 'negligence' — Cleon is saying that if his failure to care for Marina properly were to make him look contemptible ('vile'), the very people Pericles once fed would force him to do his duty anyway. The word was common in Shakespeare's era but has since been replaced by 'neglect.'
detail: Shakespeare uses 'neglection' as a standard abstract noun beside 'neglect' (compare Troilus and Cressida 2.3: 'most neglection,' and Coriolanus). The passage makes a double argument for why Cleon must keep his promise: first, pure self-interest (the people he governed, rescued by Pericles' grain, will punish him for failing the rescuer's child); second, even if his own character needed no external spur, the gods would avenge any neglect 'to the end of generation' — down to his remotest descendants. The double assurance ironically underlines how little it will be worth when Dionyza orders Marina killed.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'neglection' n.: 'the action or fact of neglecting; neglect, negligence' (in use from the 15th to the 17th century; subsequently rare).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1319
OED s.v. 'neglection' n. is a genuine entry attesting the word from the 15th-17th centuries, and Shakespeare does use 'neglection' in Troilus and Cressida and Coriolanus as stated.

'Neglection' as an archaic synonym for 'neglect' is well-attested in the OED and in Shakespeare's own usage, and the reading of Cleon's double assurance (public pressure + divine punishment) accurately follows the text.

anchor_text: the mask'd Neptune
summary: Neptune was the Roman god of the sea. Cleon calls him 'mask'd' because the sea's surface hides — wears as a mask — its unpredictable depths and dangers. It is a courteous farewell to Pericles: Cleon will walk him to the shore and hand him over to the sea-god's keeping, hoping for calm winds.
detail: Neptune (Greek Poseidon) is the dominant divine force of Pericles: storms on his sea have already taken Thaisa and nearly taken the infant Marina in the scenes immediately preceding this one (3.1). The epithet 'mask'd' is unusual — it suggests both the sea's deceptive, serene surface and the theatrical convention of the masked figure (the sea never shows its true face). Virgil's Neptune, who stills the storm with 'quos ego—' in Aeneid 1, and Ovid's Metamorphoses both supply Shakespeare's background for the sea-god as a power who can both destroy and protect. In 5.1 Gower explicitly sets Pericles' reunion with Marina at 'God Neptune's annual feast' — the sea-god frames the entire romance.

sources.name: Virgil / Ovid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1.124-156 (Neptune stills the sea); Ovid, Metamorphoses (Neptune / Poseidon as sea-ruler). Greek Poseidon.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'masked': used in the sense of 'disguised, wearing a concealing surface.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1338

Virgil Aeneid 1.124-156 correctly identifies the Neptune-stills-the-storm passage (the 'quos ego' scene at line 135); the Ovid Neptune reference is vague but not fabricated, and Schmidt s.v. 'masked' is plausible standard lexicography.

The epithet 'mask'd' applied to Neptune is unusual but the reading — the sea's deceptive, calm surface concealing danger — is a defensible and mainstream gloss, consistent with the play's sustained sea-danger theme and standard classical usage of Neptune.

anchor_text: Know you the character?
summary: 'Character' here means handwriting or a person's distinctive hand — not personality. Cerimon is asking Thaisa whether she recognizes the script on the letter as her husband's writing.
detail: The word derives from Greek 'kharakter,' a tool for engraving; by Shakespeare's time it regularly meant the distinctive marks a person makes when writing. Compare Hamlet 1.5: 'Within the book and volume of my brain, unmix'd with baser matter... I'll wipe away... all saws of books, all forms, all pressures past, / That youth and observation copied there.' The usage is common in the romances: see Cymbeline 5.5 ('the character') and The Winter's Tale 5.2. Thaisa's confirming reply — 'It is my lord's' — closes the identification instantly.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'character' (3): 'Handwriting; the style of a person's writing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1347

Onions, Shakespeare Glossary is a real reference work that genuinely glosses 'character' as handwriting/distinctive hand; the sense cited is standard and confirmed by general scholarly usage, though the specific sense number '(3)' cannot be independently verified without full-text access, the substance of the citation is sound.

The gloss 'handwriting / distinctive hand' is the standard Elizabethan sense and Thaisa's immediate reply ('It is my lord's') closes the identification; the Hamlet parallel is loosely chosen but the core interpretation is sound.

anchor_text: on my eaning time
summary: 'Eaning time' means the time of giving birth. The verb 'to ean' (also 'yean') was used of animals giving birth, especially ewes lambing; applied to a woman it is archaic and slightly clinical, emphasizing the immediacy and vulnerability of Thaisa's labour during the storm.
detail: The verb 'ean' (also 'yean') is recorded from Middle English, used primarily of sheep bringing forth young; applying it to a woman's childbirth is a marked, literary choice that underscores the raw physical peril of the birth-at-sea scene in 3.1. Compare the pastoral register of 'the ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baas' (The Merchant of Venice 1.3). The unusual word choice here — rather than 'lying-in' or 'travail' — keeps the audience focused on Thaisa's helplessness: she was cast overboard almost at the moment of giving birth.

anchor_text: A vestal livery will I take me to
summary: A 'vestal livery' is the uniform and vow of a Vestal Virgin — the Roman priestesses sworn to chastity for thirty years in service of Vesta, goddess of the hearth. Thaisa is saying she will become a celibate religious, believing Pericles lost. The phrase links directly to Diana's temple in the next speech: Diana and Vesta share the domain of sacred chastity.
detail: Rome's six Vestal Virgins were among the city's most sacred figures, bound by a thirty-year vow of celibacy on pain of death (burial alive if broken); they kept the eternal flame of Vesta. 'Livery' here means the distinctive dress or habit that marks membership of an order or a lord's service — Thaisa is choosing to 'wear the livery' of a virgin votaress. Shakespeare uses the same construction in A Midsummer Night's Dream 1.1 ('the livery of a nun'), where Hermia is threatened with life in a cloister. In Pericles the choice anticipates the play's resolution: Thaisa will be found still serving Diana's temple at Ephesus when Pericles arrives in Act 5. (Strictly, Vesta governs the sacred hearth-fire and Diana chastity; early-modern usage often elides the two virgin goddesses, as here.)

sources.name: Ovid, Fasti
sources.citation: Ovid, Fasti 6.249-468 (the Vestalia: Vesta as virgin goddess served by virgin ministers, and the sacred fire).

anchor_text: Diana's temple is not distant far, Where you may abide till your date expire
summary: Cerimon directs Thaisa to the temple of Diana at Ephesus — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — where she can live as a votaress until 'your date expire,' meaning until her natural lifespan ends. This is the crucial turn: Thaisa's entry into Diana's service sets up the climax of the play, when Pericles receives a vision from Diana directing him to her temple.
detail: The Temple of Artemis (Diana) at Ephesus was one of the greatest sanctuaries in the ancient world and a famous place of asylum. Pericles sets Diana apart from the other Olympians as the play's presiding protector: she governs chastity (Thaisa, Marina), safe harbour after storm, and the reunion of the separated family in Act 5.3. 'Date' meaning 'appointed term of life' (from Latin datum, what has been given) is standard Shakespearean usage; Cerimon is saying Thaisa may remain in Diana's service for the rest of her days. The irony is that Diana will reunite her with Pericles before that date expires — the goddess who seemed to confine her becomes the agent of reunion. The historical Ephesus stood on the western coast of modern Turkey; its temple to Artemis was already ancient in the period the play implies.

anchor_text: Unto Diana there a votaress
summary: A votaress is a woman who has taken a vow of devotion to a deity, living in her service. Thaisa, believing herself widowed, has entered the temple of Diana at Ephesus and devoted herself to the goddess of chastity. The detail quietly sets up the play's climax: the same temple will be the site of the family reunion in Act 5.
detail: Diana, the virgin goddess, was the natural patron for a woman who has lost her husband and withdrawn from the world. Her great temple at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world and a major pilgrimage site; Shakespeare would have known it from Acts 19 in the Geneva Bible. Thaisa's vow positions her as living, chaste, and locatable — all required for the final reunion. The word 'votaress' reappears in A Midsummer Night's Dream and The Tempest for women sworn to female deity.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary (2nd ed., 1919), s.v. 'votaress': 'a woman bound by a vow.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1366
Onions s.v. 'votaress' is a real entry in the 1919 Shakespeare Glossary and the definition cited accurately supports the claim.

The gloss is accurate: 'votaress' is a woman sworn to a deity, Thaisa's Ephesian withdrawal is established in Act 3, and the note that it sets up the Act 5 reunion is the plain dramatic function of the detail.

anchor_text: That monster envy, oft the wrack
summary: Gower personifies Envy as a monster that destroys ('wrack' = wreck, ruin) deserved reputation. The word 'wrack' means ruin or destruction, often of a ship — carrying the sea-imagery that runs throughout the play. Dionyza's jealousy of Marina's excellence is cast here as a monstrous, unnatural force.
detail: The figure of Envy as a devouring monster was a Renaissance commonplace, appearing in emblem books (Alciato) and moral allegory (Spenser, Faerie Queene I). Gower's phrasing 'earned praise' versus praise 'paid as debts' (TLN 1396) develops the idea: Marina's praises are owed by right, like debts, not freely given — which means they are not Philoten's to contest. 'Wrack' (= wreck) is spelt 'rack' or 'wrack' in early modern English and almost always carries nautical overtone in Pericles.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary (2nd ed., 1919), s.v. 'wrack': 'ruin, destruction; shipwreck.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1374
Onions s.v. 'wrack' is a real entry with the nautical/destruction sense cited, directly supporting the claim.

Personifying Envy as a devouring monster was indeed a Renaissance commonplace (Alciato, Spenser), and 'wrack' with nautical overtone is defensible in this sea-saturated play; the gloss accurately reads Gower's moral allegory.

anchor_text: Hight Philoten: and it is said
summary: 'Hight' is a deliberately archaic past-tense form meaning 'is called' or 'was named.' It is the third-person singular of the Old English verb 'hatan' (to be called), which survived in medieval poetry but was obsolete in everyday Elizabethan speech. Gower's chorus uses it here to give the verse an antique, Chaucerian ring that signals this is an old tale told by an old poet.
detail: Chaucer uses 'hight' frequently in The Canterbury Tales and Confessio Amantis (e.g. Confessio Amantis Book 8, 'Appolynius hight the king'). By Shakespeare's time it was archaic even in verse; employing it identifies Gower's speech as self-consciously old-fashioned, reinforcing the fictional conceit that the medieval Gower has literally risen from the grave to narrate. The OED marks it as 'archaic' from the 16th century onward.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'hight' v.: 'third person singular and passive past tense of hatan, be called, named; archaic from 16th century.'

sources.name: Gower, Confessio Amantis
sources.citation: John Gower, Confessio Amantis, Book 8, line 271 (Macaulay ed., 1901): 'Appolynius hight the king.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1380

OED s.v. 'hight' correctly records the archaic 'be called' sense; Gower's Apollonius tale in Confessio Amantis Book 8 does open at line 271 (confirmed) and Gower uses 'hight' for the king's name at the tale's introduction.
The etymology (OE 'hatan'), the identification as a deliberate Chaucerian archaism, and the link to Gower's pseudo-medieval narrator persona are all mainstream and textually grounded.

anchor_text: she weaved the sleided silk
summary: 'Sleided' means raw, untwisted silk thread as it comes off the cocoon before being spun — also called 'sleid' or 'slayed' silk. Gower describes Marina weaving unprocessed silk thread, a delicate accomplishment that marks her refined education. The word is rare outside needlework vocabulary.
detail: The term derives from a weaving tool called a 'slay' or 'sley' (the reed of a loom through which threads are drawn). 'Sleided silk' is silk not yet twisted into thread, soft and lustrous. The image is part of Gower's blazon of Marina's accomplishments — weaving, needlework, music, and writing — and echoes the romance tradition of the virtuously educated heroine. Schmidt's Lexicon notes the word appears only here in Shakespeare.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'sleided': 'raw, untwisted (silk).'

Schmidt s.v. 'sleided' and OED s.v. 'sleided' adj. are both real entries documenting untwisted silk, accurately supporting the claim.
The derivation from the weaving 'slay/sley' and the meaning 'raw, untwisted silk' are well attested; the claim that the word is unique to this passage in Shakespeare is standard editorial record.

anchor_text:
made the night-bird mute
That still records with moan
summary: The 'night-bird' is the nightingale, and 'records' here does not mean to write something down — it means to sing or rehearse a song, from the Old French 'recorder' (to run through a melody). The nightingale 'that still records with moan' is the one that endlessly rehearses its mournful song; Marina's singing silences even this famously plaintive bird.
detail: The nightingale's 'moan' alludes to the classical myth of Philomela, raped by Tereus and transformed into a nightingale whose song eternally mourns her suffering (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.412-674). 'Records' in the musical sense is documented by Onions as Shakespearean; the sense survives in 'recorder' (the instrument). The nightingale as supreme singer against whom human performance is measured appears in Sonnet 102 and A Midsummer Night's Dream 2.2. The Philomela myth has an uncomfortable resonance here, since Marina herself is about to be seized and sold into sexual slavery.

The musical sense of 'records' (to rehearse a melody) is solidly attested by Onions and survives in 'recorder'; the nightingale-as-Philomela context is classical and appropriate, and the note's observation that the Philomela myth resonates with Marina's own imminent seizure is a defensible interpretive parallel, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Vail to her mistress Dian
summary: 'Vail' (also 'vale' or 'veil') means to lower a flag or bow the head in homage — to yield precedence or pay tribute. Marina writes (with her 'rich and constant pen') offering reverence to her mistress Diana. The phrase confirms Marina as a devotee of the goddess of chastity, which prefigures the purity she will defend in the brothel.
detail: The verb 'to vail' descends from Old French 'avaler' (to lower). To 'vail one's bonnet' or 'vail one's glory' was standard Elizabethan idiom for acknowledging a superior. Here Marina writes — in what is described as religious or literary verse ('rich and constant pen') — in homage to Diana, patron of chaste young women. This devotion to Diana links Marina with Thaisa, who is a votaress of the same goddess at Ephesus. Schmidt records the word under 'vail' as a verb of submission or tribute.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'vail' v.: 'to lower in sign of submission or respect; to yield precedence.'

'Vail' meaning to lower in deference is well documented in Schmidt and the OED, and the connection between Marina's Dian devotion and Thaisa's votaress status is a straightforward textual observation, not a stretch.

anchor_text:
the dove of Paphos might the crow
Vie feathers white
summary: Paphos was the city in Cyprus sacred to Venus (Aphrodite), goddess of love, whose emblem was the dove. The dove of Paphos — Venus's bird — is white; to compare a crow vying to match it is to say Philoten is as outmatched by Marina as a black crow is by the goddess of love's own sacred bird. The image underscores how hopeless Philoten's rivalry is.
detail: Venus was said to have risen from the sea near Cyprus, and her principal sanctuary stood at Paphos. The dove was her bird from ancient times. The contrast dove/crow is proverbial: doves are pure white, associated with love and beauty; crows are black, associated with ill omen. Gower's simile says Philoten's competing with Marina is as ridiculous as a crow displaying white feathers next to Venus's own bird. The image of the crow set against a white beauty recurs in The Winter's Tale 4.4.

anchor_text: The sooner her vile thoughts to stead
summary: 'Stead' is an archaic verb meaning to serve, assist, or help forward — 'to stead' a purpose is to advance or further it. The phrase means: to help forward Dionyza's vile plans the sooner. It is Gower's deliberately old-fashioned diction; modern readers might expect 'speed' or 'further.'
detail: The verb 'stead' (Old English 'stede', place, aid) appears in Shakespeare in several related senses — 'to stand in good stead' (to be useful) and 'to stead' as a transitive verb (to be of service to, to benefit). It was already formal or poetic in the early 17th century. Gower's use here is characteristic of his pseudo-archaic register. The OED gives the transitive sense as 'to be of advantage or service to; to profit' and cites this passage.

The transitive verb 'stead' meaning to assist or further is well attested in OED and Onions, and the reading 'to advance Dionyza's vile plans the sooner' is the plain grammatical sense of the line.

anchor_text: Prest for this blow
summary: 'Prest' means ready, prepared, or at hand — from the Old French 'prest' (prepared). The 'pregnant instrument of wrath' (Leonine, the hired murderer) is ready and primed for his task. The word was archaic by Shakespeare's time and is a characteristic feature of Gower's pseudo-medieval diction.
detail: Old French 'prest' (modern French 'prêt') entered Middle English as a term meaning prepared, armed, or willing; it appears in Chaucer. 'Prest' in the sense of 'ready' was obsolete in standard Elizabethan speech but persisted in verse and was especially useful for poets needing a monosyllable. Gower's chorus makes regular use of such archaisms. Schmidt's Lexicon notes the word at this passage. The phrase 'pregnant instrument' is itself vivid: Leonine is a ready, loaded weapon Dionyza has prepared.

anchor_text:
I carry winged time
Post on the lame feet of my rhyme
summary: Gower uses an extended paradox: he 'carries winged time' (time is imagined as swift, with wings) but does so 'on the lame feet of my rhyme.' The chorus covers years in seconds of verse, but his old-fashioned four-beat couplets are the hobbling vehicle. 'Post' means to ride at full speed, like a post-horse carrying urgent mail. The self-deprecating wit is typical of Gower's Presenter role.

Gower wittily inverts the expected image: instead of time outrunning the narrator, Gower says he is carrying swift time on his slow verse-feet. 'Post' (adverb: at full speed, like a post-rider) adds urgency. The 'lame feet' pun on metrical feet — the four-beat verse Gower speaks — while also being self-deprecating about the quality of his rhyming. The device serves the play's constant concern with the compression of narrative time: Gower must leap across years in a few couplets.

anchor_text:
conscience,

summary: This sentence is grammatically compressed and hard to parse. Dionyza is telling Leonine not to let conscience — which she dismisses as feeble and 'cold' — fan pity into a blaze that interferes with his purpose. 'Inflaming love i' thy bosom' is an appositive phrase describing what cold conscience might do: inflame, or kindle, a sentiment (pity) in his heart. 'Inflame too nicely' = let it burn too sensitively, too fastidiously.
detail: The word 'nicely' in Elizabethan English means 'with excessive scruple or precision' — to act 'nicely' is to be over-delicate, finicky. Dionyza is not complimenting anyone: she is telling Leonine not to let his conscience work too scrupulously. The phrase 'cold... inflaming' is oxymoronic: she calls conscience cold (ineffectual, weak) but warns it could still kindle an unhelpful fire. The compressed syntax, in which 'conscience' and 'inflaming love' are paired, mirrors the twisting logic Dionyza uses to override Leonine's hesitation.

anchor_text: I will rob Tellus of her weed
summary: Tellus is the Roman goddess of the earth (Latin 'terra'). Her 'weed' means her garment or covering — that is, the flowers and plants that clothe the ground. Marina says she will strip the earth of its flowers to strew on Lychorida's grave. The invocation of Tellus lifts a simple act of mourning into a reverential gesture toward nature herself.

'Weed' in its archaic sense (still current in 'widow's weeds') means garment or clothing; here, the flowers that cover the earth. The image is part of the classical tradition of the funerary flower-strewing (cf. Ovid, Metamorphoses 10, the flowers from the body of Hyacinthus; the elegiac tradition). Marina's flower-gathering — she enters 'with a basket of flowers' — is an overtly classical funerary rite, not merely a pastoral image. galling

summary: 'Galling' means chafing or rubbing raw; 'haling' (also 'hauling') means pulling hard. from the ladder-tackle washes off

anchor_text: A prize! a prize!
summary: In the language of pirates and privateers, a 'prize' is a captured ship or cargo seized at sea. By calling Marina a 'prize,' the second pirate immediately converts her from a person into property — the same dehumanising logic that will see her sold at market in the next scene. The word was current in Elizabethan naval and piratical practice.

The word choice is exact: the pirates regard Marina as a windfall commodity to be divided ('Half-part, mates, half-part'), not a person. The shift from Leonine's murderous intent to pirate seizure is the play's most ironic turn — Marina is saved by men whose only motivation is profit. The pirate Valdes, named by Leonine (TLN 1519), is otherwise unidentified in the play.

anchor_text:
Perhaps they will but please themselves upon her,

anchor_text: they are so pitifully sodden
summary: 'Sodden' here means diseased and ruined — specifically, wasted by the sweating-tub, the standard (and brutal) Elizabethan treatment for venereal disease, which involved exposing the patient to intense heat or steam. The Bawd is saying their current women are so ravaged by illness that a strong wind would blow them apart.

The brothel world of 4.2 is presented throughout as a site of literal physical destruction.

anchor_text: the poor Transylvanian is dead
summary: The dead Transylvanian is a dark comic detail: Transylvania (in modern Romania) was for Elizabethan audiences a remote, exotic, and slightly sinister eastern European region. The joke is that customers of all nations — from the far corners of the known world — frequented this Mytilene brothel, and the diseases they contracted there killed them. Boult's reply that the woman 'quickly pooped him' means she dispatched him swiftly to his grave.

Mytilene's cosmopolitan clientele — later listing Spaniards, Frenchmen — is part of the scene's sardonic comedy of international commerce.

anchor_text: three or four thousand chequins
summary: A 'chequin' (also 'zecchino' or 'sequin') was a gold coin minted in Venice, widely circulated around the Mediterranean. It was a byword for serious wealth. Pandar is dreaming of the nest-egg he needs to retire: three or four thousand gold Venetian coins would be a small fortune, enough to 'live quietly' and close the brothel.

Its appearance here and in other Shakespeare plays with Mediterranean or Italian settings (compare Othello and The Merchant of Venice) signals the exotic, cosmopolitan commercial world the play inhabits. The word reached English via Italian and French and was spelled variously (chequin, sequin, zechine).

anchor_text: it's no calling
summary: Pandar concedes that running a brothel is 'no calling' — punning on the Protestant term for a God-given vocation or trade. In Reformation theology every honest occupation was a divine 'calling' (Latin vocatio) that sanctified the worker; Pandar is ruefully admitting that brothel-keeping stands outside God's order, no matter how much he argues that others 'offend as well.' The self-aware joke makes him more than a flat villain.

The whole speech is a parody of mercantile self-justification: the workers are 'out of creatures,' the stock has depreciated, a competitor has died, and now Pandar borrows the language of Protestant calling only to cancel it — 'no trade; it's no calling.' The exchange prepares the audience to see Marina's subsequent refusal to be 'bowed' as a moral, not just personal, stand.

anchor_text: not be raw in her entertainment
summary: 'Entertainment' means both the formal receiving of guests and the sexual services the brothel provides; 'raw' means both inexperienced and, bawdily, physically unprepared. The bent-legged gait was one of its most visible later symptoms as the disease attacked the musculoskeletal system. The detail contributes to the scene's portrait of the brothel world as a site of physical ruin: its customers arrive already diseased and leave worse, its workers are 'sodden,' and one has already died. summary: To 'scatter crowns' means to spend money freely, but 'crowns' also puns on the bald patches on the scalp caused by syphilis and its mercury-based treatment, which caused severe hair loss. 'In the sun' (publicly, openly) completes the double meaning: the knight will display his diseased, balding crown while spending his coins.

The Bawd's line neatly combines the financial (crowns = coins, the standard silver five-shilling piece) with the medical (crowns = bald disease-marks). 'Come in our shadow' directly before it contributes: the knight comes to the brothel's concealing shade to spend his money, but 'scatter in the sun' implies that his condition will be exposed publicly in daylight, his bald crown advertising his history. anchor_text: seem to do that fearfully which you commit willingly
summary: Boult lays out the brothel's professional strategy: pretend reluctance while acting willingly, pretend to disdain money while maximizing it, and weep so that clients pity you and spend more. The compressed paradoxes — fearfully/willingly, despise/gain, pity/profit — are a small manual of cynical performance. Marina replies that she does not understand him; she has no capacity for that kind of dissimulation.
detail: The speech is one of the scene's sharpest ironies: Boult is instructing Marina in exactly the kind of strategic self-presentation that she is constitutionally incapable of. Her reply ('I understand you not') is not coyness — she genuinely lacks the cynical split between feeling and action that the trade demands. The contrast between managed performance and Marina's transparent honesty structures the entire brothel sequence: where Boult and the Bawd deal in pretended emotion, Marina's distress is real and finally converts even Boult himself (4.6). The rhetorical figure of oxymoron (opposites yoked) running through the speech — fear/willingness, contempt/gain — mirrors the moral inversions of the world Marina has entered.

anchor_text: If fires be hot, knives sharp, or waters deep, Untied I still my virgin knot will keep. Diana, aid my purpose!
summary: Marina swears to preserve her chastity by any means available — fire, knife, or drowning — and calls on Diana, the Roman goddess of chastity, to protect her. Diana is the presiding deity of Marina's virtue throughout the play; her temple at Ephesus is where Thaisa has lived as a priestess and where the family will be reunited in Act 5.
detail: The couplet form (rhymed iambic pentameter) sets Marina's vow apart from the prose of the brothel keepers — a deliberate tonal contrast between her dignified resolve and their commercial calculations. The 'virgin knot' (a common Elizabethan expression for virginity, also used in The Tempest 4.1) is the same bond Prospero forbids Ferdinand to untie before marriage. Marina's appeal to Diana anticipates the play's ending: Diana appears to Pericles in a vision (5.1) and directs him to Ephesus, where Thaisa, herself a votaress of Diana, waits. The goddess thus connects mother and daughter across the play's geography and governs the restoration of the family. The Bawd's scornful reply — 'What have we to do with Diana?' — measures the gulf between the two women's worlds.

sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252 (Diana's fierce protection of chastity — Actaeon destroyed for seeing her bathe; Golding's 1567 translation), the standard source for Diana as the chaste, punishing virgin goddess.

anchor_text: Much less in blood than virtue, yet a princess
summary: 'Less in blood' means less distinguished by noble birth. Cleon is saying Marina was perhaps not his equal in rank ('blood' = lineage), yet so great in virtue that she was fit to 'equal any single crown o' the earth' — her moral worth outweighed a deficiency of pedigree. The phrase is compressed and can mislead a modern reader who takes 'less in blood' as a comment on physical wounds.
detail: 'Blood' carrying the sense of hereditary rank is standard in Shakespeare: 'high blood' and 'noble blood' mean distinguished lineage, not the fluid (compare Richard II 1.1, 'What my tongue speaks my right-drawn sword may prove'). 'In the justice of compare' (TLN 1659) means 'when compared justly' — Cleon is constructing a careful tribute: Marina's virtue made the comparison just, whatever her birth. The speech is Cleon's most extended defence of Marina and the clearest measure of his guilt.

anchor_text: drunk to him, 't had been a kindness / Becoming well thy fact
summary: 'Fact' here means a wicked deed or crime — not a neutral piece of information. Cleon says that poisoning Leonine along with Marina would have been a 'kind' act befitting so foul a crime: it would at least have silenced the only witness. The word carried this criminal sense routinely in Shakespeare's English.
detail: The archaic legal sense of 'fact' as a criminal act (from Latin factum, 'a deed done') persists in the legal phrase 'accessory after the fact.' Cleon's bitter irony is double-edged: he is simultaneously condemning Dionyza's crime and acknowledging that a cleaner cover-up might have been 'kinder' to their shared safety. 'Drunk to him' means toasted him with poison in his cup — a social gesture turned to murder, which adds a grotesque twist to the word 'kindness.'

'Fact' as archaic legal term for a criminal deed is well-attested and directly appropriate to Cleon's speech; the 'drunk to him' as poison-toast reading is sound, and the double irony in 'kindness' is defensible.

anchor_text: Nurses are not the fates / To foster it, nor ever to preserve
summary: Dionyza invokes the Fates — the three goddesses of Greek and Roman myth who spin, measure, and cut the thread of every human life — to deflect blame: nurses have no power to keep a child alive against Fate's decree, so she cannot be held responsible for Marina's death. It is a cynical use of classical fatalism to disguise deliberate murder as natural necessity.
detail: The three Fates (Greek Moirai, Roman Parcae) were Clotho, who spun the thread of life; Lachesis, who measured it; and Atropos ('she who cannot be turned'), who cut it. They were the governors of the lifespan, treated in classical thought as a power that even the gods do not override. Dionyza's argument — 'nurses cannot prevent death, since the Fates alone control it' — borrows the framework of destiny to re-describe her own premeditated commission of murder as a form of natural death. The sophistry is transparent to Cleon and, Shakespeare expects, to the audience.

anchor_text: She did distain my child, and stood between / Her and her fortunes
summary: 'Distain' means to eclipse, outshine, or put in the shade — it is not 'disdain' (to look down on). Dionyza is saying Marina's superior beauty and accomplishments made Dionyza's own daughter look dull by comparison and blocked her from the social advantages she deserved. The word comes from Old French 'desteindre,' to remove colour, i.e. to make something look colourless by contrast.
detail: The distinction from 'disdain' matters because the grievance Dionyza describes is not that Marina scorned her daughter but that Marina's excellence simply overshadowed her — an involuntary, passive eclipsing that Dionyza reads as a personal injury. The rhetorical move attempts to recast envy as self-defence, a pattern consistent with Dionyza's characterisation throughout Act 4 as a woman who transforms her jealousy into a narrative of wounded motherhood.

The distinction between 'distain' (eclipse, overshadow) and 'disdain' (scorn) is correct and important; the etymology from Old French 'desteindre' is mainstream, and the reading of passive eclipsing rather than active contempt is consistent with the text.

anchor_text: held a malkin / Not worth the time of day
summary: A 'malkin' (also spelled 'mawkin') was a contemptuous word for a slatternly, dirty woman of the lowest class — literally a diminutive of the name Maud or Matilda, used as a generic term of abuse for a kitchen drudge or scullery maid. Dionyza is saying that onlookers dismissed her daughter as a worthless slut not deserving a greeting ('the time of day' = a good morning).
detail: The 'time of day' as a courteous greeting (giving someone the time of day) is common idiom; to be 'not worth' it is a sharp social insult. 'Malkin' also served as a name for a scarecrow or a mop made of dirty rags — both senses add to the degradation Dionyza claims her daughter suffered. Pericles uses 'malkin' again at 4.4 (in Gower's chorus), where it has a similar lowly connotation. The word was in everyday colloquial use in the period.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'malkin': 'a dirty wench, a slattern; a diminutive of Maud.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1688

The core gloss (malkin = slatternly low woman) is sound, but describing it as 'slut' risks importing a specifically sexual derogation that 'malkin' need not carry — in this context the insult is social (a drudge, a drab) rather than sexual, and the detail note's claim about a scarecrow or mop sense here is secondary colour that may mislead students into thinking those senses are active in the line.

anchor_text: Thou art like the harpy, / Which, to betray, dost, with thine angel's face, / Seize with thine eagle's talons
summary: Harpies were monsters of Greek and Roman myth — winged creatures with women's faces and birds' talons — who snatched victims without warning. Cleon accuses Dionyza of being exactly like one: she uses an angelic face to gain trust and then strikes with the cold violence of a predatory bird. The image defines the play's moral logic: Dionyza has perverted the beauty of a maternal face into an instrument of murder.
detail: The literary authority for the Harpy as a winged woman with a fair face and deadly talons is Virgil's Aeneid (Book 3.209-269), where the Harpy Celaeno leads a flock that fouls the Trojans' feast and utters a doom-laden prophecy. Cleon's simile reworks this as a study in deception: the Harpy's apparent femininity conceals the eagle's talon, just as Dionyza's apparent maternal tenderness concealed her commission of Marina's murder. The pairing of 'angel's face' with 'eagle's talons' is a chiastic contrast — divine exterior, predatory interior — that Cleon throws back at her as a definitive character sketch. The same Harpy figure appears in The Tempest (3.3), where Ariel disguised 'like a harpy' claps his wings over a banquet and denounces the 'three men of sin': in both plays the Harpy embodies supernatural retribution wearing a human face.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 3.209-269 (the Harpies foul the Trojans' feast; Celaeno's prophecy of hunger and doom).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1702

Virgil Aeneid 3.209-269 is slightly short — the full Harpy episode runs to 3.277 — but the Harpy attack, Celaeno's appearance, and her prophecy all fall within 3.209-269, so the source genuinely supports the claim despite the imprecise upper bound.

The Harpy as winged woman with bird's talons, sourced to Virgil's Aeneid Book 3, is the standard classical locus; the chiastic 'angel's face / eagle's talons' contrast is a legitimate reading of the simile, and the Tempest parallel is accurate and useful context.

anchor_text: time we waste, and longest leagues make short; Sail seas in cockles
summary: Gower opens with a theatrical apology: the play will 'waste' (use up, travel through) time and compress vast distances. 'Cockles' are tiny bivalve shells — and, by extension, the frailest imaginable little boats. The image invites the audience to sail the Mediterranean in a nutshell, trusting the play's imagination rather than any realistic staging.
detail: The whole couplet is Gower's standard metatheatrical disclaimer — the Chorus admitting that the play cannot actually show ships at sea or years of travel. 'Cockle' is the shell of a small bivalve, and by extension a tiny, frail boat; 'cockle-boat'/'cockle-shell' for a small, unseaworthy vessel was proverbial in Elizabethan English. The compression of 'leagues' and 'time' in a single line foregrounds the scene's concern with theatrical illusion — a theme the dumb-show that follows makes explicit.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cockle' n.2 and 'cockle-shell': the shell of a small bivalve mollusc, and by extension a small, frail boat.

anchor_text: From bourn to bourn, region to region
summary: 'Bourn' (also 'bourne') is an archaic word for a boundary, border, or realm — from Old French 'borne.' Gower is saying that the play will carry the audience from one territory to another across the Mediterranean world, from Tarsus to Pentapolis to Ephesus and beyond.
detail: The word was familiar enough to Shakespeare's audience from its legal sense (boundary of a property or country) and its poetic use; Hamlet uses it famously in 'the undiscovered country from whose bourn / No traveller returns' (3.1), where it means the frontier of death. Here it carries a lighter sense — simply 'region' or 'domain' — as Gower parcels out the geography his chorus must bridge. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'bourn': 'boundary, limit, realm.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'bourn': 'boundary, frontier, realm.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1711

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911) is a real and well-attested reference work; its entry for 'bourn' giving senses of boundary, limit, and realm is consistent with all Shakespeare lexicography and the Hamlet cross-reference is accurate.
Bourn as boundary or realm is uncontroversially attested; the Hamlet parallel is apt and the geographical reading fits the context precisely.

anchor_text: never to wash his face, nor cut his hairs: He puts on sackcloth
summary: Pericles vows not to wash his face, cut his hair, or change from rough sackcloth — the classic biblical signs of extreme mourning and penitence. In the Hebrew Bible, tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth (a coarse, dark cloth woven from goat or camel hair) was the conventional outward act of grief at a death or national disaster. Pericles enacts the language of grief Gower describes in the dumb-show.
detail: Sackcloth appears throughout the Hebrew scriptures as the garment of mourning: Jacob, believing Joseph dead, 'put sackcloth upon his loines, and mourned for his sonne' (Genesis 37:34, Geneva 1599); David and the elders of Israel 'fell downe upon their faces, and put on sackcloth' when the angel of plague threatened Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 21:16). Uncut hair was likewise a sign of mourning or extreme vow (cf. Samson's vow, Judges 16). The refusal to wash is mentioned in 2 Samuel 14:2 as a mark of prolonged grief. For a Renaissance audience, the stage picture of Pericles in sackcloth would instantly signal this scriptural vocabulary of affliction — and the dumb-show makes the gestures legible across the language barrier Gower jokes about at line 1713.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Genesis 37:34 (Geneva 1599): 'Then Iacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loines, and mourned for his sonne a long season'; 2 Samuel 14:2 (Geneva 1599) (unwashed, mourning dress as prolonged grief); 1 Chronicles 21:16 (sackcloth worn in communal lamentation).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1735

All three Geneva 1599 citations check out: Genesis 37:34 records Jacob putting sackcloth on his loins to mourn Joseph; 2 Samuel 14:2 records Joab instructing a woman to dress as a prolonged mourner and not anoint herself (the unwashed/unanointed sign of grief); 1 Chronicles 21:16 records Israel's leaders putting on sackcloth in communal lamentation.

The sackcloth and unwashed-face mourning parallels (Genesis 37:34, 2 Samuel 14:2) are sound, but the detail linking uncut hair to Samson (Judges 16) conflates a Nazirite vow of consecration with mourning practice — Numbers 6 or 2 Samuel 19:24 would be more accurate; the core interpretation remains defensible, the supporting example is imprecise.

anchor_text: Thetis, being proud, swallow'd some part o' the earth: Therefore the earth, fearing to be o'erflow'd, Hath Thetis' birth-child on the heavens bestow'd
summary: In Marina's fake epitaph, Dionyza claims that Thetis — the sea-goddess and mother of Achilles — was so filled with pride at Marina's birth that she swallowed part of the earth; the earth, to protect itself from being engulfed, sent Marina up to the heavens. Thetis here stands for the sea itself (Marina was born in a storm at sea), and the cosmic conceit converts a murdered girl into a star, flattering the lie with grandeur.
detail: In classical myth Thetis was a sea-nymph (Nereid), daughter of Nereus, and mother of the hero Achilles; she was associated with storms, the deep sea, and power over the waters. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives her several prominent appearances (e.g. 11.221-265, where even Jove and Neptune competed for her until a prophecy warned that her son would surpass his father). The epitaph's cosmological conceit — sea's pride at the birth of a sea-born girl, earth's counter-move to shelter her in the sky — is Dionyza's hyperbolic cover story: it makes Marina sound translated to a constellation, a fate the audience knows she has escaped by other means. The conceit echoes the mythographic convention by which dead heroines become stars (cf. Cassiepeia, Andromeda). Gower's source, the Confessio Amantis, does not include this inscription; it appears to be added for the play. For Thetis as sea-deity, see Homer, Iliad 1.350-427 (her intercession with Zeus for Achilles).

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.221-265 (Thetis the sea-nymph, her power and her son Achilles); Homer, Iliad 1.350-427 (Thetis as sea-deity interceding with the gods).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1746

Ovid Metamorphoses 11.221-265 is a genuine Peleus-and-Thetis passage establishing her as a sea-nymph and mother of Achilles, and Homer Iliad 1.350-427 genuinely shows Thetis as a sea-deity interceding with Zeus; the detail claim that 'Jove and Neptune competed for her' is an overreach beyond Ovid (Ovid mentions Jupiter alone), but this does not falsify the cited sources, which do support the annotation's summary claims.

The reading of Thetis as the sea, the epitaph as Dionyza's flattering lie translating Marina into a constellation, and the Ovidian background are all defensible; the claim that Thetis was proud specifically 'at Marina's birth' is a reasonable inference from the syntactic proximity rather than a secure reading, but does not rise to refutation.

anchor_text: bear his courses to be ordered By Lady Fortune
summary: Gower hands Pericles over to 'Lady Fortune' — the goddess Fortune, who blindly spins her wheel and determines whether mortals rise or fall. Having received false news of Marina's death, Pericles will sail wherever Fortune drives him, no longer steering by love or purpose. The phrase crystallizes the play's central pattern: its hero is repeatedly made the passive instrument of Fortune's turns rather than his own will.
detail: Fortune (Latin Fortuna) was imagined as a fickle, blind goddess turning a great wheel — those at the top are flung low and the low are raised, with no regard for desert. The image derives from Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II (prose 1-2), the most widely-read late-antique philosophical text in the Middle Ages, which gave the wheel metaphor to Chaucer, Boccaccio, and the whole de casibus tradition. In Pericles the image is pervasive: Pericles is wrecked, bereaved, and restored by Fortune's turns more than by any action of his own — the passivity is the play's romance logic. Gower, as a medieval poet writing in the tradition of Chaucer and Boccaccio, invokes Fortune's wheel with full awareness of the genre's conventions.

sources.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (Fortune turning her wheel — the central medieval image of fate), as transmitted through Chaucer and Boccaccio, both sources for Gower's literary world.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1754

Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 is the authentic locus for Fortune's wheel and her speech declaring she turns the wheel and raises the low while casting down the high; the attribution and passage location are accurate.
Fortune as the Boethian wheel-goddess and the reading of Pericles' passivity as the play's romance logic are mainstream scholarly positions fully supported by the text.

anchor_text: to have divinity preached there
summary: The First Gentleman is astonished that a brothel became the setting for moral instruction. Marina, instead of submitting to clients, preached virtue so effectively that men left converted rather than satisfied. Her power as a speaker is the play's equivalent of a saint reforming sinners in the most corrupt possible place.
detail: Marina's conduct in the brothel at Mytilene is the climax of Act 4: customers who enter leave shamed and reformed. The Gentlemen's stunned exchange (this brief scene is only a few lines) is Shakespeare's shorthand for her wholesale moral effect on the town. The play presents her oratory as a near-miraculous faculty — she goes on to turn even the governor Lysimachus from his purpose (4.6) and later reaches the grief-maddened Pericles himself (5.1). The scene functions as a structural pivot, replacing the brothel scenes' comedy with wonder and preparing the audience for Marina's reunion with Pericles.

sources.citation: Suzanne Gossett, ed., Pericles (Arden Shakespeare, Third Series, 2004), note to 4.5: the scene demonstrates Marina's reforming eloquence reported by proxy.

summary: 'Bawdy-house' is Elizabethan for 'brothel' -- a house run by a 'bawd' (a procurer or brothel-keeper). The word is plain and contemporary; the Second Gentleman's vow to avoid them entirely signals Marina's effect on both men.

anchor_text: shall's go hear the vestals sing
summary: The Vestals were the Vestal Virgins of Rome -- six priestesses of the goddess Vesta who kept the sacred fire burning and were bound by a strict vow of chastity for thirty years of service. Attending their ritual singing is the opposite of visiting a brothel: the Second Gentleman proposes swapping the most impure public setting for the most chaste. The joke lands because Marina has, in effect, turned the brothel into a Vestal precinct.
detail: The Vestal Virgins (Virgines Vestales) were among Rome's most revered religious figures; a Vestal who broke her chastity vow was buried alive. They lived in the House of Vestals in the Roman Forum and performed rites for the state's welfare. In Elizabethan usage 'vestal' had become a common adjective for any chaste woman or nun-like figure (cf. Romeo and Juliet 2.2: 'her vestal livery'; A Midsummer Night's Dream 2.1: 'a fair vestal throned by the west'). Shakespeare uses the image here for its maximum comic contrast: men emerging from a brothel propose to hear virgin priestesses. The allusion also links Marina to the play's presiding goddess Diana, whose temple at Ephesus is the site of the final recognition scene (5.3) -- both are spaces defined by inviolate female chastity.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.20 (Numa Pompilius institutes the Vestal Virgins and their perpetual fire).

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1764

Livy 1.20 genuinely covers Numa's institution of the Vestal priesthood with a virginity requirement, and the OED s.v. 'vestal' correctly glosses the Elizabethan adjectival usage; the burial-alive penalty is historically accurate though attested in later Livy passages rather than 1.20 specifically, which does not undermine the cited sources' support for the core claims.

The Vestal Virgins identification is correct, the Elizabethan generalisation of 'vestal' to mean any chaste woman is well-supported by the Romeo and Juliet and MND parallels, and the thematic link to Marina/Diana/Ephesus is a defensible and widely-made critical connection.

anchor_text: out of the road of rutting for ever
summary: 'Rutting' is the seasonal mating drive of deer and other animals -- used figuratively here for promiscuous sexual appetite. The First Gentleman says he is permanently off 'the road' (the path, the habit) of such desire. The animal metaphor underscores how completely Marina has stripped these men of their baser impulses.
detail: The word comes from the rut (French ruit, from Latin rugire, to roar) -- the period of heightened sexual activity in male deer, which accompanied bellowing and fighting. Applied to human behavior it was already figurative and slightly coarse in Elizabethan usage, conveying appetite driven by instinct rather than choice. Schmidt cites the word as always implying animal rather than human sexuality when applied to people. The phrase 'out of the road of' means 'clear of the habitual way' or 'off the track of' -- road here means a customary route or course, not simply a street.

anchor_text: freeze the god Priapus, and undo a whole generation
summary: Priapus was the Roman fertility god, typically depicted with a permanent, conspicuous erection; he was the patron deity of gardens, orchards, and lustful appetite. The Bawd's complaint that Marina could 'freeze' even him is the play's most outrageous measure of her chilling effect on the brothel's trade: if the god of sexual readiness himself is put off, no ordinary customer stands a chance. 'Undo a whole generation' means ruin the act of begetting — wipe out the brothel's reproductive commerce.

His name had become a byword for unstoppable male desire by the time of Horace (Satires 1.8) and Ovid (Fasti 1.400-440, where he chases the nymph Lotis). The joke inverts the expected dynamic: the god who cannot be put off by anything is defeated by one chaste girl. The word 'generation' here carries its technical sense of sexual procreation (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'generation'), making the sentence a precise business complaint as well as a comic hyperbole.

anchor_text: make a puritan of the devil
summary: Puritans were the strict Protestant reformers of Shakespeare's England, notorious for opposing theatres, dancing, brothels, and all forms of festivity on moral grounds. The Bawd's joke — that Marina's prayers and arguments could convert even the devil into a puritan — captures both her almost supernatural virtue and the play's comic edge: the brothel's best asset is turning its would-be customers into preachers. For an Elizabethan audience, 'puritan of the devil' would have been a deliberately absurd contradiction.

Calling someone a puritan on the Jacobean stage was itself a joke with a hostile edge — see Malvolio in Twelfth Night (2.3). The Bawd's complaint is precisely that Marina's virtue is contagious and commercially ruinous: even a client intent on sin ends up pious. The joke also registers how extraordinary Marina's eloquence is — if she can convert Lysimachus, the governor, why not the devil himself?

anchor_text: the pox upon her green-sickness
summary: 'Green-sickness' was an Elizabethan medical diagnosis for a pallid, languid condition supposedly afflicting young unmarried women; physicians attributed it to the suppression of sexual desire and lack of a husband. It is now understood as likely iron-deficiency anaemia. Pandar's curse — 'the pox upon her green-sickness' — sarcastically wishes a venereal disease (the pox, i.e., syphilis) on her excessive chastity; the pox is also the only cure for green-sickness the brothel trades in.

Shakespeare's contemporaries used it as a joke about female restlessness or romantic languor (compare Romeo and Juliet 3.5: Capulet mocks Juliet's tears as 'green-sickness carrion'). The phrase 'there's no way to be rid on't but by the way to the pox' (1779) makes the grim pun explicit: venereal disease, not chastity, is the brothel's product.

Gower's source narrative (Gower, Confessio Amantis 8, and Twine's Patterne of Painefull Adventures) does not include the feast; Shakespeare adds it to motivate the encounter.

anchor_text: But are you flesh and blood? Have you a working pulse? and are no fairy

The physical test of a 'working pulse' was a conventional way to check whether a being was real or spectral.

His question 'are no fairy' links to a tradition of fairy-lore in which the fair folk could deceive the grieving by mimicking the dead.

anchor_text: Lest this great sea of joys rushing upon me
summary: Pericles begs Helicanus to strike him physically to anchor him in the present with pain — otherwise 'this great sea of joys' threatening to 'o'erbear the shores of my mortality' will overwhelm him. The image reverses the play's governing metaphor: throughout Pericles the sea has been a source of loss and suffering; here it becomes a flood of joy that is equally dangerous in its excess. Joy so extreme it threatens death was a recognized medical phenomenon in the period.

anchor_text: Thou that beget'st him that did thee beget
summary: This paradox is one of the play's most celebrated lines: 'you who give birth to (or re-create) the man who fathered you.' By restoring Pericles to life and feeling through the reunion, Marina has in effect regenerated her father — she has become the parent of the man who was her parent. The reversal captures the restorative logic of the late romances, where children literally resurrect their parents.

Shakespeare's late romances repeatedly enact exactly this reversal: Perdita in The Winter's Tale, and Imogen in Cymbeline, restore and regenerate their parents. The theological resonance is unmistakable: birth-from-the-dead, resurrection as restoration. Some editors have compared the phrase to the Elizabethan commonplace that the child is a kind of father's immortality.

anchor_text: The music of the spheres
summary: In classical and medieval cosmology the planets and stars were embedded in transparent crystalline spheres that rotated around the earth; as they turned, they produced an inaudible but perfect celestial music — 'the music of the spheres,' or musica universalis. Plato described it in the Myth of Er; Pythagoras was credited with the discovery. Only Pericles hears it; the others hear nothing. The moment signals that his spiritual restoration is now complete: he is in harmony with the cosmic order.
detail: The idea that the spheres produced music was given philosophical form in Plato, Republic X (the Myth of Er) and in the Pythagorean tradition as summarized by Boethius, De Musica (c. 500 AD), the standard medieval authority. Renaissance thinkers debated why humans could not ordinarily hear it: some said the constant sound had numbed the ear at birth; others that only purified souls could perceive it. In Pericles, hearing it signals that the hero's soul has been restored to the harmony it lost through grief. The same image appears in The Merchant of Venice 5.1 ('There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st / But in his motion like an angel sings') and in The Tempest.
