anchor_text: thick slumber Hangs upon mine eyes
summary: Immediately after hearing the music of the spheres, Pericles falls into a deep, sudden sleep. This supernatural sleep prepares the audience for Diana's vision: in classical and biblical tradition, divine visions came to mortals during sleep (the dream-vision was the standard narrative form for heavenly messages). The 'thick slumber' is not ordinary tiredness but the divinely induced unconsciousness that precedes revelation.
detail: The vision that follows belongs to the classical and medieval genre of the dream-vision (Lat. visio), in which a deity or allegorical figure appears to a sleeping protagonist. Classical examples include the dreams in Virgil's Aeneid (Aeneas's vision of Anchises, Dido, Creusa); the genre was codified by Macrobius in the Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis (c. 400 AD). In Pericles the stage direction 'Diana appears to Pericles as in a vision' signals this is a recognized narrative device, not a hallucination.

anchor_text: My temple stands in Ephesus: hie thee thither
summary: Diana appears to Pericles in a vision and directs him to her temple at Ephesus, where Thaisa has been living as a priestess since Cerimon revived her. The great temple of Artemis (Diana) at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, the most famous sanctuary of the goddess in the Greek world. The vision is the play's final divine intervention, directing Pericles toward the reunion that will complete the family's restoration.
detail: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus (the Artemision) was destroyed and rebuilt several times; in its classical form it was a massive marble structure. The Acts of the Apostles (19:23-41) describes the silversmith's riot at Ephesus in defense of 'great Diana of the Ephesians' against Paul — so Shakespeare's audience would recognize the city as a center of Diana worship. In the play's symbolic structure, Diana represents both chastity (which Marina preserved against the brothel) and restoration: Thaisa's becoming Diana's votaress is both her survival strategy and a form of spiritual preservation. The circle is closed when Pericles arrives at Diana's temple to tell his story and find his wife.

The Artemision at Ephesus as one of the Seven Wonders and its association with chastity/restoration in the play's symbolic structure are well-founded; the Acts of the Apostles reference is a legitimate gloss on audience recognition.

anchor_text: hither come so soon, Is by your fancy's thankful doom
summary: 'Doom' here means judgment or decision, not death or destruction. 'Fancy' means imagination. anchor_text: Hail, Dian! to perform thy just command
summary: Pericles addresses Diana, the goddess of chastity and the moon, whose temple at Ephesus is the scene's setting. Thaisa, who has lived as the goddess's high priestess, stands before him.

Ovid's Metamorphoses (1.476-477 and 3.155-252) and Hesiod's Theogony (918) are the background sources; Diana's silver color ('wears yet thy silver livery,' line 2297) refers to her identification with the silver moon.

anchor_text: your present kindness Makes my past miseries sports

The extreme reversal — misery become sport — is a rhetorical figure of antithesis that measures the scale of the restoration.

Compare the same figure in The Winter's Tale 5.3 ('redeems all sorrow') and Lear 5.3's impossible reunion with Cordelia. Pericles immediately modulates to the wish for annihilation — to 'Melt and no more be seen' — which shows how close overwhelm and dissolution are to each other in this moment.

anchor_text: on the touching of her lips I may Melt and no more be seen. O, come, be buried A second time within these arms

Then he shifts to 'be buried... within these arms': an embrace as a second burial, echoing the first burial when he cast her in the sea-chest. The figure belongs to the language of the late romances, where joy and grief are structurally interchangeable.

anchor_text: In Antiochus and his daughter you have heard Of monstrous lust the due and just reward

This ending deliberately echoes the morality-play tradition in which characters were abstractions of virtue or vice rather than individuals. Gower's archaic couplets ('you have heard / reward') reinforce the deliberately old-fashioned, authoritative tone of a poet who stands outside the story and pronounces its meaning.

anchor_text: For wicked Cleon and his wife, when fame Had spread their cursed deed, and honour'd name Of Pericles, to rage the city turn, That him and his they in his palace burn
summary: This passage is grammatically compressed. The sense is: when rumor ('fame') had spread Cleon and Dionyza's crime (their attempted murder of Marina) and Pericles' honored name, the people of Tarsus turned to rage and burned Cleon and Dionyza inside their palace. 'To rage' is used as a noun in apposition to 'the city' — the city turned into rage. 'Him and his' means Cleon and his wife. None of this is shown onstage; Gower narrates it as swift divine retribution.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1886), s.v. 'fame': 'report, rumor, public talk.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2398
Schmidt s.v. 'fame' as 'report, rumor, public talk' is a correct and standard Schmidt definition for this archaic sense.

The syntax gloss is broadly correct, but the note's claim that 'to rage' is 'a noun in apposition to the city' is a grammatical misdescription — 'to rage' is a predicate complement or result phrase ('turned to rage'), not an appositive noun; the sense given is right but the grammatical label is inaccurate enough to warrant caution.

anchor_text: The gods for murder seemed so content To punish them although not done but meant
summary: Gower states that the gods saw fit to punish Cleon and Dionyza for the murder of Marina even though it was not actually carried out — the pirates seized her before Leonine could strike. 'Content' here means satisfied, pleased — the gods were willing to punish intention as equal to the act. The moral is a sharp one: evil intent is enough to bring divine punishment, a doctrine in tension with legal practice (which generally requires an act, not merely a plan) but consistent with the play's providential framework.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1886), s.v. 'content' adj.: 'satisfied, pleased, willing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2402
Schmidt s.v. 'content' adj. ('satisfied, pleased, willing') is a real and correct Schmidt entry for this usage.

'Content' as satisfied/willing is correct; the observation that punishing intended but unexecuted murder is morally sharper than legal practice is a defensible and conventional reading of the play's providential framework, not an overreach.

anchor_text: on your patence evermore attending, New joy wait on you! Here our play has ending
summary: 'Patence' is Gower's archaic spelling of 'patience,' in keeping with his deliberately old-fashioned diction throughout the play. 'Evermore attending' means always waiting upon, always in attendance on — he has been the audience's patient guide through the whole long story. The Epilogue ends with a direct blessing to the audience ('New joy wait on you'), a conventional closure of medieval narrative performance, and a self-aware closing tag ('Here our play has ending') that returns us from the fictional world to the theatre.

sources.name: OED

sources.name: John Gower, Confessio Amantis
sources.citation: John Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390): Gower's characteristic archaic four-beat rhyming couplets and medieval narrative-closure formulas.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2404

OED does list historical variant spellings of 'patience' (including 'patence') and the Confessio Amantis citation is real and correct; the note about Chaucerian orthography is editorial interpretation but not a fabricated claim.

'Patence' as archaic spelling of patience, the convention of a direct audience blessing to close a medieval-style narrative, and the self-aware theatrical tag are all well-supported; the claim of 'Chaucerian orthography' is a slight embellishment (it is Gower's own archaic diction, not specifically Chaucer's), but not materially wrong.
